The New York City teahouse Soft Hours opened in May with the goal of helping visitors explore the diversity of tea. | James K Lowe/Soft Hours

In Los Angeles, Tea at Shiloh describes itself as a “late night teahouse.” Here, visitors can reserve slots from 7 to 11 p.m. to sip unlimited amounts of tea — at this hour, all herbal, with blends made by each day’s staff — and sprawl out in nooks of plush cushions, in a warmly lit loft with tall ceilings and exposed brick, while jazz musicians play in a corner. “I was looking for soft spaces in the evening,” says founder Shiloh Enoki, who opened the eponymous teahouse in 2022.

Enoki previously worked in the music industry, and her experience with nightlife was often loud and centered on the more performative aspects of dating (“being perceived by guys,” she says). For her new venture, “All I wanted to do was drink tea, listen to jazz, be cozy, and still have the opportunity to meet strangers.” Tea felt like a conduit to an alternative space. While coffee shops tend to encourage a practice of grab and go, or of work or hustle culture, “that’s not the energy of tea,” according to Enoki. “Tea is like, I’m gonna sit here for hours and I’m gonna have a deep conversation with the person sitting across from me, and that’s so rare in our culture.”

Despite tea’s astounding popularity globally, the United States has long lagged behind many other countries when it comes to tea consumption, and that conception of tea has mostly been limited to iced black tea. This, however, appears to be changing, with the U.S. importing far more tea — in the hundreds of millions of dollars — this decade than it did 30 years ago, with millennials in particular the most likely to be tea drinkers. Matcha is, obviously, everywhere; according to the New Consumer, it usurped chai as the leading specialty tea drink in cafes. A lot more tea, it seems, is about to follow, as new tea-focused businesses sprout up across the country and as tea sees increased applications as a flavor element in food, desserts, and cocktails in addition to its consumption as a standalone drink.

Across the country, teahouses with a similar ethos to Enoki’s are catering to the desire for another kind of space: one that feels slower and more intentional than the average coffee shop, and which offers a different experience than yet another restaurant or high-end cocktail bar. In July, “tea salon” Han Cha opened in Chicago, serving a selection of nine teas from Chicago-based tea company Spirit in the format of British high tea. Over the course of the two-hour-long booking, guests might sip Taiwanese black tea with notes of quince and orange blossom alongside bites of English cheddar and Korean-style quick pickles, or Thai white tea with Japanese curry pimento cheese sandwiches.

Heiji Black, who partnered with artist Theaster Gates (in whose Stony Island Arts Bank building the concept is located) on the venture, is compelled by the way tea “makes people slow down and savor the experience.” She cites the teahouses she grew up going to in Korea, which were “really about being social and meeting with people and connecting with them,” as inspiration for Han Cha.

At Tea at Shiloh, Enoki also tries to emphasize being in the moment. While the cafe welcomes co-working, especially during the day, she says she wanted to design the experience at night such that people “don’t want to be on their laptop or their phone.” Rather than enforce a hard no-laptop policy, Tea at Shiloh offers other things for people to do with their hands, like games, clay, and watercolors. The dim lighting and communal seating also offer “subtle cues” that the space, at night, isn’t a place for being lost in a screen, she explains.

Even teahouses that don’t serve matcha, like Tea at Shiloh, cite its importance in the current teahouse moment. In May, the artist Juno Shen opened Soft Hours, a teahouse in Manhattan’s Chinatown. (A laptop-free space, it draws inspiration from the Song dynasty, which Shen describes as a “culturally rich era” in which scholars “built rituals around slowing down and shifting your attention.”) “Matcha and boba have done something really important in making tea culture relevant to a younger generation, and I think we’re reaching a point where people are asking, What else is there?” Shen says. At Soft Hours, there is no matcha whisked in front of you, poised for a TikTok video. Likewise, “we don’t do boba; we don’t do cold foam. We moved away from all the performance that a trendy tea place would have.”

Instead, Shen’s menu hews toward a selection of Chinese teas: streamlined but still showing range. There’s green tea fragrant with jasmine; two kinds of oolong, one oxidized in a way that gives it notes of plum and the other roasted over charcoal until it evokes toasted nuts; black tea with a honey-like body; and a deeply woodsy fermented pu’erh. Perhaps the main concession to trends is that every tea can be ordered as an iced latte as well, which Shen considers a way for people to “softly get introduced” to tea. “I’m not presenting something that’s extremely traditional, so I think I’m just the next step of [people] exploring a little bit more about tea,” Shen says. “I think the next stage of tea culture in America should move beyond individual ingredients becoming trendy [and into] the understanding of tea as this incredibly diverse seasonal category.”

Tian Tea House opened in Kansas City, Missouri, in late 2025. Matcha drinks are far and away the most popular, according to co-owner Saranya Hubbard. “I really don’t have to advertise anything that much — it already sells itself,” she says. But similarly to Shen, Hubbard, who grew up in Thailand surrounded by the tea culture in Bangkok’s Chinatown, sees her teahouse as an opportunity to showcase the wider variety of Asian tea culture. Tian brews and offers classes on Chinese gongfu tea and serves lesser-known Thai tea, including one made with hibiscus and bael (a fruit that’s sometimes called golden apple or stone apple). To make the most of the space, the teahouse turns into Moon, a cocktail bar, at night. Tea bridges the gap between the two concepts: There are highballs infused with tea and whisky drinks made with matcha.

Further proof of tea’s rising moment can be found in Heytea’s current expansion across the United States. The Chinese chain got global attention when it popularized cheese tea in the late 2010s, but it didn’t enter the U.S. market until 2023, when it opened its first store in NYC; now, it has more than 40 locations nationwide. With drinks like milk tea boba, fruit teas with inclusions, and black teas finished with fluffy toppings, the chain sits at the intersection of the growing cultural fixations on bubble tea, matcha, and highly customized specialty beverages of all kinds, including coffee and dirty soda. The chain describes itself as offering “new-style” tea, which senior PR manager Yinnan Shen explains to mean “experimenting a lot with what tea can become.” Some of its beverages, Shen says, take the approach of crafting a cocktail: What botanics can be added to the drink? What layers of texture and flavor? McDonald’s Sweet Tea this is not.

In June, Heytea also opened the first U.S. location of its Teabar offshoot. The concept — which serves dine-in only pots of tea as well as tea ice cream and elaborate beverages like jasmine milk tea topped with a “matcha cloud” — rapidly drew massive crowds. Unlike Heytea shops, which offer a more grab-and-go feel, Teabar was, like some of those independent teahouses, intended to be more of a place to slow down. Together, the interest in Teabar in addition to the original Heytea concept, represent what Shen calls tea’s “continued evolution.” “What Heytea is trying to do is find the most accurate contemporary interpretation of people’s needs around tea,” she says. That seems especially pertinent in the context of the U.S., where the tea culture is nascent compared to China.

Now, according to Nethra Rajendran, a beverage experience developer at Oatly, black tea, jasmine, and oolong are starting to “re-emerge in new formats,” particularly in mainstream chains. Instead of boba being the medium for these flavors, they’re increasingly popping up as part of the growing “refresher” category,” she explains.

Of course, the interest in tea is no longer limited to the teahouse or tea bar alone. “We can see a very real application of tea beyond a [drink] base in the 2025 resurgence of Earl Grey,” wrote Rajendran, noting the popularity of Earl Grey syrups and creamtops for use in matcha and coffee drinks. Tea is no longer a standalone drink, but, increasingly, a freeform flavor element. When NYC’s ambitious new soft serve shop Unnecessary opened this summer, it launched with a “not-so-plain vanilla,” enriched with osmanthus oolong. Oolong also appears as the grounding basenote of its watermelon-mint flavor, which it developed to be more refreshing than what people might expect from typical milk tea.

The argument has been made that we, as modern society, are on a hedonistic hunt for more flavors, our tastebuds “spoiled” by the glut of “maple-matcha-blackberry-thyme-yuzu-miso-caramel everything.” Every drink is involved in a way that only the early days of the Starbucks Frappuccino could have foretold; every dish is a referential mashup of a handful of other dishes or other cultural fascinations. Perhaps tea, with its global breadth barely tapped in the U.S., can provide further flavors to mine. Nearly every culture has a tea to explore, Rajendran adds: the osmanthus and oolong of East Asia, the masala chai and Assam teas of South Asia, the rooibos and kineliba of Africa, the hibiscus in the Caribbean and Latin America, the sweet tea of the American South.

Tea has been around for thousands of years, but perhaps we’ve yet to see how far it can continue to go. As Heytea’s Shen says, “Tea is a living culture, and living culture changes.”

items.text:
When it comes to finding gifts for people who love to cook, I stand by a simple gift shopping mantra: Know what your giftee likes, and then expand upon (or improve) their area of interest. Meaning, if they’re always tracking down rare spices, gift them a pirate’s hoard of blends from one of our favorite places to buy spices online; if they love to bake, equip them with a charming set of nontoxic, miniature muffin baking pans. And so on and so forth; basically, pay attention to what needs an upgrade in their life (there’s a good chance it’s cooking utensils) and which knives aren’t cutting it in their rotation.

Whether you’re shopping on a budget or looking for a splurge-worthy piece of cookware or bundle of pantry staples, we’ve got the gift for you and the picky cook that you love.

A sleek Japanese santoku knife

I think of a santoku as the sexier version of a classic chef’s knife, because while it’s designed to handle meat, fish, and vegetables like a pro, a santoku blade is often a bit lighter on its feet (read: cutting board) that other styles of do-it-all knives. This particular option from Mercer Culinary is a line cook favorite.


Mercer Culinary M20707 Genesis 7-Inch Santoku Knife

Where to Buy:

$39.95 at Mercer Culinary Store


This artisan-made molcajete

If your giftee is always on the literal grind for their recipes, chances are they could use a molcajete, a traditional Mexican mortar and pestle. This large, 9-inch version was made in collaboration with the third-generation stone artisan Don Enrique of San Salvador El Seco, Puebla, and includes a particularly cool, graphic tejolote (grinding pestle).


Masienda Molcajete

Where to Buy:

$95 at Masienda


Fancy tinned tomatoes

Row 7 has made quite a stir in the food world this year. Founded in 2018, the organic seed and food company is the brainchild of chef Dan Barber, plant breeder Michael Mazourek, and seedsman Matthew Goldfarb, and was initially focused on collaborating with farmers on a smaller scale in order to produce more flavor-focused (as opposed to maximum output-focused) produce. This last winter, folks yielded the fruits of their labor; a line of complex, flavor-packed tinned veggies was launched, including my personal favorite, the tinned tomatoes. They’re bright, jammy, and an absolute indulgence. Just what gifts are for.


Row 7 Sweet Prince Tomato Tins (3 Pack)

Where to Buy:

$29 at Row 7


This hand cream dethrones Aesop

If you love someone who loves to cook, their hands could probably use some love, too. Monastery’s everything balm (I use it on my hands and dry legs) feels like the love child of Aesop and Aquaphor, because it’s equal parts unisex, herbaceous remedy and non-fuss, non-greasy (and non-overly-perfumed) clear balm. The little silver tube is also the most giftable of hand creams for my money, complete with an antique-looking tube roller key for squeezing out every last drop.


Monastery Universal Balm

Where to Buy:

$48 at Monastery


The more cool Finnish dish towels, the merrier

Finnish design house Marimekko is one of Eater staffers’ absolute favorite brands for pops of color and graphic design, and this striking towel duo would make a great, seasonal-spanning addition to any cook’s kitchen.


Marimekko Unikko Organic Cotton Kitchen Towels

Where to Buy:

$52 at Amazon


Nordic Ware sheet pans

There are certainly cuter sheet pans out there, but aesthetics are a low priority when it comes to good, always-reach-for-it bakeware. Seasoned cooks and bakers know: It’s all about the straightforward functionality of Nordic Ware. Irresistibly affordable at $40 for a set of three (including a tiny quarter-sheet that’s great for organizing mise en place and baking just a cookie or two from the freezer), these sheet pans bake evenly and resist rust and warping. Best of all, they last, unlike all the wonky nonstick sheet pans we’ve put up with in the past.


Naturals 3 Piece Baker’s Delight Set

Where to Buy:

$40 $36.9 at Amazon

$40 at Nordic Ware


This cottagecore apron is doing so many things right

This, folks, is what happens when you create a charming apron with substance. The midweight cotton material checks the box for durability, while avoiding the stiffness that sometimes comes with other self-declared tough aprons. There are two extra large pockets for all of your tools, and, perhaps my favorite feature of all, a cross-back design, so you don’t have to worry about re-tying and adjusting your apron strings.


Big Night Gingham Smock Apron

Where to Buy:

$55 at Big Night


Do they love spicy food? Stock their pantry with high-quality staples

Flamingo Estate has earned its place in the olive oil hall of fame for its Martha Stewart-approved heritage olive oil, and it recently started infusing its liquid gold with guajillo chiles to add a bit of fruity heat to the versatile, peppery olive oil. The spicy heritage EVOO is also sold with its smoked chipotle chile crisp as part of a very giftable duo.


Flamingo Estate Spicy Finishing Set

Where to Buy:

$108 at Flamingo Estate


Versatile glassware

Bustling home kitchens often beget broken glassware. As someone who loves to host, I keep a cabinet of tall tumblers stocked for birthday parties, barbecues, and dinners and brunches at home. This robust set of 14-ounce crystal tumblers from the Eater x Zwiesel Fortessa collaboration can handsomely serve everything from juice to batch cocktails.


Eater x Zwiesel Fortessa Modus Crystal 14-oz Glass (Set of 8)

Where to Buy:

$47.95 at Amazon


A supply of beans

Beans, like all pantry staples, have gotten upgrade in recent years. Primary Beans is a company that promotes lesser-known bean varieties (see their not-a-pinto set). If you’ve ever been skeptical of whether fresher beans really matter, these flavorful beans — which cite their harvest dates with pride — will remove any doubt. They’ll make an especially good gift for a cook looking to diversify their protein sources.


Primary Beans “All the Beans” Set

Where to Buy:

$144.86 at Primary Beans


Spices you can’t find at every grocery store

There’s an entire Eater guide to shopping for spices online, but some of my favorite picks come from Shop Palestine and Hayati; the former is a project of the Middle East Children’s Alliance, a nonprofit working to support the rights and the wellbeing of children in Gaza by amplifying products from the region, such as this za’atar, harvested from the hills of Palestine. Hayati, meanwhile, is a newcomer to the spice scene that was founded by Palestinian-American Yasmine Borno with the goal of highlighting distinctly Palestinian flavors; she sources Hayati’s za’atar ingredients from the same spice shop in Palestine that was beloved by her own great-grandparents.


Shop Palestine Baladna Za’atar (12 oz)

Where to Buy:

$12 at Shop Palestine

Hayati Green Za’atar

Where to Buy:

$11.99 at Hayati


The Bentley of cutting boards

I have yet to find a cutting board that can outdo a John Boos in matters of durability and function; the sustainably sourced maple, cherry, and walnut boards have been made by the same Midwest-based company since 1887, and while its fine craftsmanship can easily boost the boards’ price tags to $100+, there are some beautiful, more affordable options out there, such as this limited-counter-space-friendly, 1-inch thick, square format cutting board.


John Boos Cutting Board (12”x12”)

Where to Buy:

$59.95 at Amazon


Six months of pasta

Whether it’s bougie hand soap, merino wool socks, or artisanal pasta, high-end everyday items are always a good gift, especially for someone who doesn’t tend to treat themselves. Sfoglini’s bronze-cut pasta, made from a range of grains including einkorn and rye, is extruded through bronze dies into a variety of specialty shapes before being slow-dried. The result is a slightly rougher (and overall better) texture that holds its shape. This subscription includes two shipments of six boxes of pasta — some for now, some for later.


Sfoglini

Where to Buy:

$110 at Sfoglini


A bread chopping board

What do you get the cook who has everything? That’s when you start troubleshooting hyperspecific culinary problems you imagine they’re having. So, save a bread lover from the constant tyranny of crumbs with this handy slotted cutting board. Its many wide divots will catch the shards from their crustiest baguettes, and every errant seed from their most-flecked loaves. You just solved a problem they didn’t realize needed solving.


Dyke & Dean Chopping Board

Where to Buy:

$25 at Dyke & Dean


Miniature muffin pans for the avid baker

Making muffins can be so satisfying under any circumstances, but The Borrowers-size cinnamon nut muffins in a trio of light pink miniature muffin pans? The dream.


Caraway Mini Muffin Pan Trio

Where to Buy:

$125 at Caraway


This Funfetti-esque spatula set

Admittedly, I still have a few scratched-up plastic spatulas floating around my kitchen. But given the potential health risks of black plastic utensils, there has never been a better time to help swap out your gifted culinary pal’s tools with Get It Right’s nontoxic, microplastic-free silicone cooking accessories. This speckled, Funfetti-esque spatula set looks good enough to eat.


Get It Right 3-Piece Sprinkles Spatula Set

Where to Buy:

$34.95 at Get It Right


Soaps for home cooks are officially chic now

I’m a big fan of fancy hand soaps — just one of life’s everyday sensory luxuries — and recently, the concept of swish soaps specifically designed to live at the kitchen sink have been catching my eye; Naomi makes a lightly exfoliating, bergamot and pepper hand soap that is formulated to banish the garlic odor from your fingertips while also looking quite chic by your sink.


Naomi After-Cooking Hand Scrub (Bergamot & Pepper)

Where to Buy:

$29 $27 at Amazon


A magnetic wood trivet

In her debut cookbook The Secret of Cooking, Bee Wilson gives more credit than most to the humble trivet: “Without them [in addition to discard bowls, she writes], the whole business of cooking is so much trickier than it needs to be.” While a basic trivet does the job, consider giving the gift of a magnetic trivet. Skip the awkward maneuvering of carrying a hot, heavy dish to the dining table and use a trivet that attaches itself to the bottom of the pot instead. This one is designed for a Staub Dutch oven, but Le Creuset makes one as well.


Staub Magnetic Wood Trivet (9-inch)

Where to Buy:

$44.99 at Zwilling


A pair of squeeze bottles

Home cooks are increasingly adopting what chefs have long known — that squeeze bottles give you the most control over your oils, vinegars, and sauces while cooking, not to mention the perfect drizzles and drops while plating. (At this point, we’re all well aware of that social media-famous squeeze bottle of olive oil.) OXO’s squeeze bottles, which come in two sizes, have attached hinged caps for easy one-handed use.


OXO 6-oz Squeeze Bottles (3 Pack)

Where to Buy:

$11.19 at Walmart


A frying pan that can handle four chicken breasts

Ah, the peace of knowing that all four of my desired chicken breasts would fit, uncrowded, in this sleek pan for chicken picatta night. As lovers of quality cookware, Eater collaborated with Heritage Steel on a collection of 5-ply stainless steel pots and pans, and the line includes this much-welcome, do-it-all, 12-inch lidded skillet.


Eater x Heritage Steel Fry Pan With Lid (12-inch)

Where to Buy:

$149.95 at Heritage Steel


Soup season is almost here

Another stand out of the Eater x Heritage Steel collection is this 8-quart stock pot, which has carried me through many a soup season. The 5-ply stainless steel is incredibly durable, yet lightweight enough that I can still carry it when it’s full of ungodly amounts of chili.


Eater x Heritage Steel 8 Quart Stock Pot with Lid

Where to Buy:

$229.95 at Heritage Steel


Gold tweezers

Tweezers often end up at the butt end of jokes about fussy food. But there’s no denying they’re useful in the kitchen doing what tongs can, but, in many instances, better. items.text:
The fall cookbook season is here | Collage: Masood Shah

We have reached that time of year again. Every good tomato suddenly prompts the pondering: Will this be the last one for the season? The heat begins to give way to crisper breezes, and we start to crave the comfort of windows fogged up from bubbling pots of soup instead of thinking about how to minimize our time in front of a hot stove.

Luckily, this season’s cookbooks offer many exciting ways to joyously warm ourselves in the kitchen, whether by baking border-traversing croissants and comforting counter cakes, or keeping the stove simmering with Dutch ovens of borscht, beef noodle soup, or budae jjigae. There are diversions from the standard cookbook on this list, too, like a divorce-inspired reflection (in which the essays are just as essential as the recipes) and a treasure trove of a garden almanac that feels like an escape into another world. I’ve compiled 12 selections from the fall cookbook season that have me especially excited to cook and read this fall and winter.

Bake Sum: Asian American Pastries, Breads, and Other Treats

Joyce Tang with Soleil Ho

Hardie Grant, out now

If you feel like everything is an Asian American bakery now, you’re right. In the Bay Area, Bake Sum — with its Spam-musubi-esque croissants and ube pineapple buns — was an early adopter of the current trend, starting as a pandemic pop-up in 2020 before opening its Oakland location the following year. In her colorful and playful new cookbook, chief baking officer Joyce Tang pulls back the curtain on her cuisine-bending treats, like quiche inspired by chawanmushi, the Japanese savory egg custard, and danishes in the style of okonomiyaki and aloo matar, the Indian dish of spiced potatoes and peas. The bakes involving laminated dough are ambitious, weekend-worthy projects, but the book takes a welcomingly progressive approach, easing in novice bakers via puddings and jellies (its first recipe is a simple, anyone-can-do-it microwave mochi) before exploring more advanced techniques in its chapter on cakes, and then making its way to croissants. This is a book for the person who counts big baking projects among their favorite ways to spend the colder months.


Bake Sum: Asian American Pastries, Breads, and Other Treats


Where to Buy:

$34.63 at Amazon

$35 $32.62 at Bookshop


Food is a Feeling: Recipes & Stories, with Love

Carla Lalli

Clarkson Potter, out now

Lalli, who won audiences over as Carla Lalli Music during her time at Bon Appétit, has catalogued the dissolution of her 24-year marriage in a cookbook. With its reflections on motherhood, identity, and where a background in restaurants fits into those things, Lalli continues the narrative thread of releases like Tanya Bush’s Will This Make Me Happy and Rebecca May Johnson’s Small Fires. That’s to say that you’re here as much for the essays as for the recipes.

The latter, including dishes such as “weeknight lamb chop special, for any number” and “quick beans and rice for when the avocado is ripe,” are delightfully loose and flexible. These are realistic suggestions for weeknights when you’re burnt-out, but also for those glorious instances in which you care more about getting yourself on the sand than fussing about what to make for your beach trip (for those instances: peaches with lime and salt).Many of these ideas were birthed during “separation summer,” when Lalli often found herself eating alone after years of cooking for four. These recipes (and the words that accompany them, like a list of things that “made [Lalli] feel free”) will feel useful on bad days, sick days, and anytime you need to give yourself grace, but also whenever you need to be reminded of how much pleasure life offers.


Food is a Feeling: Recipes & Stories, with Love


Where to Buy:

$36 $33.41 at Amazon

$36 $33.55 at Bookshop


Flamingo Estate Pleasure Principles: An Almanac from the Garden

Richard Christiansen

Chronicle, September 15

Pleasure Principles is the newest book from Richard Christiansen of Flamingo Estate, the Los Angeles-based lifestyle brand so luxurious and sprawling in its ambitions that even Martha Stewart has described it as “over the top.” Pleasure Principles is predictably maximalist; not specifically a cookbook, it feels like picking up a paper trail while exploring the lush thicket of Christiansen’s secret (if oft-Instagrammed) garden. Stories about the building of Christiansen’s property veer into detours about the history of camellia plants and Coco Chanel, interspersed with archival imagery and photos of flora shot in the style of high-fashion editorial. A primer about the vast range of sage plants gives way to a checklist of garden tasks for January, seasonal project ideas (“help build a bird’s nest” or “make a sage tincture”), and recipes for pasta with sage leaves embedded in the dough and vegetable broth featuring lotus petals and dried skullcap. Pleasure Principles feels like an immersive fantasy world: Open up any random page for a little hit of magic, or an escape into Christiansen’s sparkly, greenery-filled universe. It’s a book that’ll make even winter feel vibrant and full of possibility.


Pleasure Principles: An Almanac from the Garden


Where to Buy:

$35 $32.62 at Amazon

$35 $32.62 at Bookshop


No. 1 Best Indian Cookbook in the World: At-Home Recipes from the Streets, Truck Stops, Villages, and Palaces of India

Meherwan Irani with Jamie Feldmar

Ten Speed Press, September 22

This is a book that will make you want to have a party. That’s partially because recipes like the deep-fried, carb-on-carb vada pav and crisp, thin dosa with coconut chutney will feed six or more (and benefit, process-wise, from the economy of scale). It’s also because it feels raucous and alive, full of bright colors, bold typography, and big proclamations, ready for joyful debate. Is vada pav, as Meherwan Irani writes, “without question, the greatest sandwich of all time”? Is this, indeed, as the title suggests, the best Indian cookbook in the world? This is food that makes you want to crowd around a table, tearing off pieces of seekh kebab with fluffy, still-steaming naan and crushing cold beers. Whether Indian street food is, as Irani audaciously claims, the “best food on the planet” remains up for discussion, but for those of us who can’t get to India or to Irani’s lauded North Carolina restaurants Chai Pani and Botiwalla anytime soon, this book is a good way to test that argument.


No. 1 Best Indian Cookbook in the World: At-Home Recipes from the Streets, Truck Stops, Villages, and Palaces of India


Where to Buy:

$40 $37.28 at Amazon

$40 $37.28 at Bookshop


Happy Snacking, Don’t Die!: Foraging and Vegan Recipes with Black Forager

Alexis Nikole Nelson with Jeanelle Hayner Olson

S&S/Simon Element, September 22

Alexis Nikole Nelson, also known as Black Forager, is a bright spot in the doom spiral that social media can often be. Nelson is known (and widely loved, picking up nearly 5 million followers on TikTok alone) for her bubbly disposition, whimsical vibe, and clever creations such as syrup infused with pine cones and color-changing pine-needle cookies. She demystifies the vast array of food that you can forage without even having to go deep into the woods, like acorns and the fruit of the linden trees that are abundant in many parts of the United States, and balances practicality, safety, and play in the process. Her long-awaited cookbook gets its name from the catchphrase that ends her videos: “Happy snacking. Don’t die.” With recipes like pickled magnolia flowers, Japanese knotweed granita, and maitake mushroom “steaks,” this book promises to be a guide to seeing even your suburban neighborhood through new eyes.


Happy Snacking, Don’t Die!: Foraging and Vegan Recipes with Black Forager


Where to Buy:

$35 $31.36 at Amazon

$35 $32.62 at Bookshop


Librae: Third-Culture Recipes from a Cult New York Bakery

Dona Murad

Quadrille, September 22

New York City’s Librae Bakery draws on its owner Dona Murad’s upbringing in Bahrain with an Indian and Portuguese mother and a Bahraini Persian father; her time spent working in Copenhagen with her husband Andre, who is French Moroccan; and her new life in NYC, where Andre grew up. Naturally, the bakery has embraced the language and perspective of “third-culture” cuisine from the start, serving croissants with pistachio frangipane, scented with rose water; morning buns spread with labneh and za’atar; babka with both lemon curd and loomi (black lime); and more.

Much of this book requires getting comfortable with Murad’s “mother dough” recipes — like ones for croissant dough, morning buns, and enriched dough — or working with sourdough starter. For those new to these more involved bakes, Murad provides thorough, nicely documented steps and imagery. If you need something easier than croissants, Murad’s cookies and breads, including cleverly topped sheets of focaccia, provide a more approachable entry point. Another book for bakers who don’t turn down a challenge, Librae is also for anyone who respects traditional pastry techniques but wants to push flavors further.


Librae: Third-Culture Recipes from a Cult New York Bakery


Where to Buy:

$43 $38.35 at Amazon

$43 $40.08 at Bookshop


Korean Soups: Recipes for Soups and Stews That Nourish, Restore, and Delight

Clara Lee and Eddo Kim

Workman, October 6

If it can’t still be summer, at least it’s almost soup season. Here, Clara Lee and Eddo Kim break Korean soups into fundamentals — a chart compares the qualities of guk versus tang versus jjigae versus jeongol; the first section of the book is about making broth, then categorizing those soups into applications. There are quick-cooking soups, soups for slower nights, soups for each season, soups that are especially restorative, and soups for sharing; you could spend the entirety of the coming colder months cooking exclusively through this repertoire. If Lee and Kim’s names are familiar, that’s because they ran the cherished San Francisco superette Queens, which closed in 2023 to transition into a line of pantry staples. The shop has been described as “iconoclastic,” representing the new wave of Korean American cuisine. Consider Korean Soups essential for anyone who loves to be cozy, anyone who’s looking to deepen their understanding of Korean home cooking, or anyone who simply needs more ways to use the gochujang they bought for cookies a while ago.


Korean Soups: Recipes for Soups and Stews That Nourish, Restore, and Delight


Where to Buy:

$32 $30 at Amazon

$32 $29.82 at Bookshop


Gather Around My Table: Simple, Flavorful Recipes from My Global Pantry

Kay Chun

Knopf, October 6

Recipe developers I know cite NYT Cooking contributor Kay Chun among their favorite recipe developers, and it’s easy to see why. Her book starts off with snacks and pickles, Chun adding low-lift but flavor-packed flourishes: She quickly marinates sardines to top toast; her calamari gets a gilda-esque zhuzh, skewered with fried peppers and olives. Gather Around My Table delivers on its promise of simple, weeknight-friendly food that doesn’t feel boring, with dishes such as grilled tofu simmered in soy sauce with aromatics, and then given the ssam and taco treatment with both a perilla leaf and a tortilla. Wakame and a shallot vinaigrette featuring grated tomatoes make her green salad livelier and less run-of-the-mill (her mustard vinaigrette, meanwhile, gets amped up by doenjang). I appreciate that Chun gives tofu an entire chapter, too, coaxing even omnivores to employ it more, as in her pork breakfast sausages with crumbled tofu for added moisture and protein. With Gather Around My Table, Chun consistently offers low-effort ways to make familiar dishes more interesting and rewarding.


Gather Around My Table: Simple, Flavorful Recipes from My Global Pantry


Where to Buy:

$40 $37.32 at Amazon

$40 $37.28 at Bookshop


Taiwanese? A Rambling Reflection on the Recipes, Cultures, and People Defining this Island

Eric Sze and Elyse Inamine

Hardie Grant, October 13

We’ve come full circle: Fusion is good again, or at least so proclaims chef Eric Sze, known for his New York City restaurant Wenwen and the recently closed 886. His debut cookbook Taiwanese?, emphasis on that question mark, is an ode to letting Taiwanese food be fun, free, and a little freaky: His lu rou fan, also known as lo ba beng, the dish of braised pork over rice, includes the “strange addition of peanut butter,” for example. Why the hell not? Especially when Sze has, as documented in the book (with vivid imagery from star photographer Alex Lau), gone on a bonkers crawl of 60-plus bowls of lu rou fan in a single week; he’s earned the right to experiment.

Taiwanese? is not the traditionalist’s guide to the cuisine, but anyone who likes seeing the commonalities between disparate cuisines and playing with the boundaries between them will get a kick out of this book, which includes recipes such as seared zhajiang lasagna with pork and octopus, and beef noodle soup burgers. Suffused throughout is an impish irreverence: Sze calls a soup made with yellow-fat chicken, regular chicken, and goth Silkie chicken “diversity chicken soup”; he’s known, at Wenwen, for the “BDSM chicken” (that incredibly involved recipe’s in here, too). Taiwanese? is a good pick for anyone who’s serious about food but also sees some of the self-imposed rules around it as really not that serious, or for anyone who’s got a great relationship with their local butcher.


Taiwanese? A Rambling Reflection on the Recipes, Cultures, and People Defining this Island


Where to Buy:

$40 $37.28 at Amazon

$40 $37.28 at Bookshop


Daily Dessert: Treats on Repeat

Caroline Schiff

Abrams, October 13

This is, as the name would suggest, a book for the daily-3-p.m.-sweet-treat kind of people. But it’s also a book about making baking less annoying and more chill, a boon for anyone who would love baked goods more often but hates the thought of all the fuss. In her new cookbook, beloved New York City pastry chef Caroline Schiff, formerly of Gage & Tollner, assures you that sifting is generally unnecessary, and that your baked goods will probably be fine even if you forgot to bring the eggs to room temperature. Her ideas will appeal to the baker without a dishwasher — her giant chocolate chip cookie dirties one bowl and requires no mixer nor hand beater. It’s also for the snacker who wants to reap as many rewards as possible out of a single burst of effort (see: the black and white coconut macaroons and the cardamom counter cake with chocolate ganache, both of which keep for a week). Schiff describes her lifestyle as one in which “there’s always something sweet in [the] kitchen — no special occasion required,” allowing friends to stop by anytime for cake and tea (and that’s both definitions of the latter). Daily Dessert is a call to be less fussy and to enjoy ourselves more, and who isn’t enticed by that?


Daily Dessert: Treats on Repeat

Lozhka: Eastern European Soups, Stews & Other Things We Eat with a Spoon

blocks.x: The fall cookbook season is here | Collage: Masood Shah

We have reached that time of year again. Every good tomato suddenly prompts the pondering: Will this be the last one for the season? The heat begins to give way to crisper breezes, and we start to crave the comfort of windows fogged up from bubbling pots of soup instead of thinking about how to minimize our time in front of a hot stove.

Luckily, this season’s cookbooks offer many exciting ways to joyously warm ourselves in the kitchen, whether by baking border-traversing croissants and comforting counter cakes, or keeping the stove simmering with Dutch ovens of borscht, beef noodle soup, or budae jjigae. There are diversions from the standard cookbook on this list, too, like a divorce-inspired reflection (in which the essays are just as essential as the recipes) and a treasure trove of a garden almanac that feels like an escape into another world. I’ve compiled 12 selections from the fall cookbook season that have me especially excited to cook and read this fall and winter.
Bake Sum: Asian American Pastries, Breads, and Other Treats
Joyce Tang with Soleil Ho
Hardie Grant, out now

If you feel like everything is an Asian American bakery now, you’re right. In the Bay Area, Bake Sum — with its Spam-musubi-esque croissants and ube pineapple buns — was an early adopter of the current trend, starting as a pandemic pop-up in 2020 before opening its Oakland location the following year. In her colorful and playful new cookbook, chief baking officer Joyce Tang pulls back the curtain on her cuisine-bending treats, like quiche inspired by chawanmushi, the Japanese savory egg custard, and danishes in the style of okonomiyaki and aloo matar, the Indian dish of spiced potatoes and peas. The bakes involving laminated dough are ambitious, weekend-worthy projects, but the book takes a welcomingly progressive approach, easing in novice bakers via puddings and jellies (its first recipe is a simple, anyone-can-do-it microwave mochi) before exploring more advanced techniques in its chapter on cakes, and then making its way to croissants. This is a book for the person who counts big baking projects among their favorite ways to spend the colder months.

Clarkson Potter, out now

Lalli, who won audiences over as Carla Lalli Music during her time at Bon Appétit, has catalogued the dissolution of her 24-year marriage in a cookbook. With its reflections on motherhood, identity, and where a background in restaurants fits into those things, Lalli continues the narrative thread of releases like Tanya Bush’s Will This Make Me Happy and Rebecca May Johnson’s Small Fires. That’s to say that you’re here as much for the essays as for the recipes.

The latter, including dishes such as “weeknight lamb chop special, for any number” and “quick beans and rice for when the avocado is ripe,” are delightfully loose and flexible. These are realistic suggestions for weeknights when you’re burnt-out, but also for those glorious instances in which you care more about getting yourself on the sand than fussing about what to make for your beach trip (for those instances: peaches with lime and salt).Many of these ideas were birthed during “separation summer,” when Lalli often found herself eating alone after years of cooking for four. These recipes (and the words that accompany them, like a list of things that “made [Lalli] feel free”) will feel useful on bad days, sick days, and anytime you need to give yourself grace, but also whenever you need to be reminded of how much pleasure life offers.

Stories about the building of Christiansen’s property veer into detours about the history of camellia plants and Coco Chanel, interspersed with archival imagery and photos of flora shot in the style of high-fashion editorial. A primer about the vast range of sage plants gives way to a checklist of garden tasks for January, seasonal project ideas (“help build a bird’s nest” or “make a sage tincture”), and recipes for pasta with sage leaves embedded in the dough and vegetable broth featuring lotus petals and dried skullcap. Pleasure Principles feels like an immersive fantasy world: Open up any random page for a little hit of magic, or an escape into Christiansen’s sparkly, greenery-filled universe. It’s also because it feels raucous and alive, full of bright colors, bold typography, and big proclamations, ready for joyful debate. Is vada pav, as Meherwan Irani writes, “without question, the greatest sandwich of all time”? Is this, indeed, as the title suggests, the best Indian cookbook in the world? This is food that makes you want to crowd around a table, tearing off pieces of seekh kebab with fluffy, still-steaming naan and crushing cold beers. Whether Indian street food is, as Irani audaciously claims, the “best food on the planet” remains up for discussion, but for those of us who can’t get to India or to Irani’s lauded North Carolina restaurants Chai Pani and Botiwalla anytime soon, this book is a good way to test that argument.

Her long-awaited cookbook gets its name from the catchphrase that ends her videos: “Happy snacking. Don’t die.” With recipes like pickled magnolia flowers, Japanese knotweed granita, and maitake mushroom “steaks,” this book promises to be a guide to seeing even your suburban neighborhood through new eyes.

New York City’s Librae Bakery draws on its owner Dona Murad’s upbringing in Bahrain with an Indian and Portuguese mother and a Bahraini Persian father; her time spent working in Copenhagen with her husband Andre, who is French Moroccan; and her new life in NYC, where Andre grew up. Much of this book requires getting comfortable with Murad’s “mother dough” recipes — like ones for croissant dough, morning buns, and enriched dough — or working with sourdough starter. For those new to these more involved bakes, Murad provides thorough, nicely documented steps and imagery. If you need something easier than croissants, Murad’s cookies and breads, including cleverly topped sheets of focaccia, provide a more approachable entry point. If it can’t still be summer, at least it’s almost soup season. There are quick-cooking soups, soups for slower nights, soups for each season, soups that are especially restorative, and soups for sharing; you could spend the entirety of the coming colder months cooking exclusively through this repertoire. If Lee and Kim’s names are familiar, that’s because they ran the cherished San Francisco superette Queens, which closed in 2023 to transition into a line of pantry staples. The shop has been described as “iconoclastic,” representing the new wave of Korean American cuisine. Kay Chun
Knopf, October 6

Recipe developers I know cite NYT Cooking contributor Kay Chun among their favorite recipe developers, and it’s easy to see why. Her book starts off with snacks and pickles, Chun adding low-lift but flavor-packed flourishes: She quickly marinates sardines to top toast; her calamari gets a gilda-esque zhuzh, skewered with fried peppers and olives. Gather Around My Table delivers on its promise of simple, weeknight-friendly food that doesn’t feel boring, with dishes such as grilled tofu simmered in soy sauce with aromatics, and then given the ssam and taco treatment with both a perilla leaf and a tortilla. Wakame and a shallot vinaigrette featuring grated tomatoes make her green salad livelier and less run-of-the-mill (her mustard vinaigrette, meanwhile, gets amped up by doenjang). I appreciate that Chun gives tofu an entire chapter, too, coaxing even omnivores to employ it more, as in her pork breakfast sausages with crumbled tofu for added moisture and protein. With Gather Around My Table, Chun consistently offers low-effort ways to make familiar dishes more interesting and rewarding.

Eric Sze and Elyse Inamine
Hardie Grant, October 13

We’ve come full circle: Fusion is good again, or at least so proclaims chef Eric Sze, known for his New York City restaurant Wenwen and the recently closed 886. His debut cookbook Taiwanese?, emphasis on that question mark, is an ode to letting Taiwanese food be fun, free, and a little freaky: His lu rou fan, also known as lo ba beng, the dish of braised pork over rice, includes the “strange addition of peanut butter,” for example. Why the hell not? Especially when Sze has, as documented in the book (with vivid imagery from star photographer Alex Lau), gone on a bonkers crawl of 60-plus bowls of lu rou fan in a single week; he’s earned the right to experiment.

Taiwanese? is not the traditionalist’s guide to the cuisine, but anyone who likes seeing the commonalities between disparate cuisines and playing with the boundaries between them will get a kick out of this book, which includes recipes such as seared zhajiang lasagna with pork and octopus, and beef noodle soup burgers. Suffused throughout is an impish irreverence: Sze calls a soup made with yellow-fat chicken, regular chicken, and goth Silkie chicken “diversity chicken soup”; he’s known, at Wenwen, for the “BDSM chicken” (that incredibly involved recipe’s in here, too). Taiwanese? is a good pick for anyone who’s serious about food but also sees some of the self-imposed rules around it as really not that serious, or for anyone who’s got a great relationship with their local butcher.
Taiwanese? A Rambling Reflection on the Recipes, Cultures, and People Defining this Island

This is, as the name would suggest, a book for the daily-3-p.m.-sweet-treat kind of people. But it’s also a book about making baking less annoying and more chill, a boon for anyone who would love baked goods more often but hates the thought of all the fuss. In her new cookbook, beloved New York City pastry chef Caroline Schiff, formerly of Gage & Tollner, assures you that sifting is generally unnecessary, and that your baked goods will probably be fine even if you forgot to bring the eggs to room temperature. Her ideas will appeal to the baker without a dishwasher — her giant chocolate chip cookie dirties one bowl and requires no mixer nor hand beater. Daily Dessert is a call to be less fussy and to enjoy ourselves more, and who isn’t enticed by that?

items.title: The Best New Restaurants in Queens
items.summary: Astoria now has a spot to satisfy soulful cravings for long-simmered Korean seolleongtang (ox bone soup). Jin Broth is a takeout counter inside the Marquee
items.text:
Astoria now has a spot to satisfy soulful cravings for long-simmered Korean seolleongtang (ox bone soup). Jin Broth is a takeout counter inside the Marquee Astoria banquet hall, which opened in May. Amid business conventions, there’s marvelous seolleongtang: thick, white, and almost creamy from all the collagen that’s seeped out from hours of simmering beef bones. It comes with the customary fixings of scallions, sea salt, and pepper so everyone can season it to their liking. Tender beef also appears in the suyuk (boiled beef slices with dips) and what the restaurant calls lasagna dumplings: squares of dumpling stuffing with the wrapper on the top and bottom.

After a decades-long hustle, Burmese Bites chef and owner Myo Lin Thway has finally opened the full-service restaurant of his dreams. The former buffet-style Point Brazil in Astoria has transformed into a cool, bustling space with quick, kind service. All the bestsellers from Thway’s days at street festivals, Queens Night Market, and Queens Center Mall now rest in beautiful, colorful ceramics and thatched wood plateware. The must-orders: the assorted palatas like the chicken curry that kickstarted the business; tea leaf salad; ohno kauswe (coconut chicken noodle soup); mohinga (ground fish noodle soup); and crispy eel chile fries.

Xiaozhan is a fantastic rice noodle soup spot with a sauce bar in Flushing, which opened in May. All ten noodle soups are served in mini clay pots with bundles of slippery, slurpy, bouncy rice noodles; vegetables; and protein options such as fish, beef, shrimp, and chicken. The soup bases vary from mushrooms to assorted chile preparations (charred, pickled, oil), but the passionfruit stands out. It has a lovely balance of robust flavors — sour, spicy, savory — brightened up with passion fruit and lemon. And if you want more spiciness or umami, head to the sauce bar. The space is tiny, and wait times can exceed an hour, so go during off-peak hours.

Northwestern Queens can now grab some good Nigerian jollof and suya with the opening of the D.C.-based takeout chain Disbe Good, which opened inside the Sunnyside Eats ghost kitchen in May. The jollof is fluffy, tomato-based, and subtly spicy. But the charcoal-grilled smokiness of the suya is loud and proud — whether you opt for the beef, chicken, or lamb. And all the meats are halal. Every order comes with an extra helping of yaji, their quality suya spice blend of peanut, smoked paprika, and chile pepper, so you can use any leftovers for your own home cooking.

Woodside has gained a thoughtful restaurant that pushes the boundaries of typical Japanese American restaurants in New York with Tomoni, which opened in April. Lunch sets include common premium offerings like wagyu or eel donburi, but the perfectly cooked protein portions are generous. But Tomoni also offers misozuke cream cheese, which has been marinated in miso for two days and served with nori and wasabi; it’s delightful: nutty and slightly sweet. There’s also the raw octopus (a small bowl of shredded octopus in a slightly vinegary seasoning) and natto (the sticky, stringy fermented soybeans usually eaten at home). It’s served with rice, sauce, a raw pasteurized egg, a couple of slices of grilled eel, tamagoyaki, and miso soup.

What looks small and divey from the front opens up into a large Chinese banquet hall-type space. Peruse a massive menu of Cantonese classics that had been sorely missing in NYC’s newest Chinatown. Fresh lobster is coated in a garlicky brown sauce. Fried whole anchovies are tossed in salt and pepper. Stellar snow pea sprouts get braised in a light savory broth, topped with fried shrimp, and served in a cast iron pot. Head over for weekday lunch specials ($14-17) on entrees like beef stew with radish and chicken with cashews — all served with soup and rice.

A new Uzbek restaurant has been doling out traditional dishes in Rego Park since April. Registan Plov Center lives up to its name with a plov that’s freshly made daily in the mornings. It’s a dome of rice, chickpeas, lamb, and cubed carrots with pops of sweetness from raisins — all tantalizingly slicked with lamb fat. Get the grilled lamb ribs, too. It’s served on a mountain of sliced lemon and tomato, topped with potato chips and a flourish of sliced onions. Wash it all down with kompot, a light seasonal fruit juice; it’s mixed berries for summer.

On the weekends, all the Forest Hills families are at the massive new location of Turkish American chain Zara, which opened in May. Of the many highlights, the huge complimentary balloon bread — that’s the length of an arm and puffed up straight out of the open-flame oven — might be the greatest. Rip into it and dip into spreads like labneh, hummus, and babaganoush. Or wrap it around grilled kababs, short ribs, and steaks. Leave room for desserts. The tas kadayif is made fresh to order: pan-fried pastry stuffed with walnuts and honey, which is served with vanilla ice cream.

items.text:
Welcome to Open Tab, a weekly roundup of the news, gossip, and stories that have stayed open in my tabs all week. Last time we covered the end of ‘Chicken Shop Date.’

Welcome back to Open Tab. Labor Day weekend was excuse enough for me to make salmon tacos with pineapple-chile salsa—always a hit—followed by a fluffy, aromatic olive oil cake. I’ve found myself cooking at home almost exclusively in recent weeks, but, in no particular order, here are the New York Restaurants I’ve been meaning to hit: Dean’s, Hommali, Kirbee’s, Graciela, and El Califa de Leon. Make of that list what you will.

This week marks 25 years since the attacks on 9/11—many in the food world are remembering Windows on the World, the restaurant opened on the top floors of the North Tower. CNN also released a documentary on the restaurant, which was at one time the highest-grossing standalone restaurant in the country.

Another fascinating read: Ruby Tandoh in the New Yorker on Saudi Arabia’s quest to rebrand as a culinary capital which includes, among other things, the introduction of Michelin stars last year. Michelin has been evaluating more and more cities, often partnering with (read: getting paid by) local tourism boards who recognize that the distinction can attract a real wave of tourists to the area. But when I interviewed him a couple years ago, Gwendal Poullennec, international director of the Michelin Guide, insisted that the guide’s expansion wasn’t about the money—it was about finding more cities with “culinary potential” than ever before.

Oh, also they’re doing $60 loaves of rye bread now. Oy.

Also in this week’s Open Tab: the people using AI agents to score reservations, what exactly are ultraprocessed foods?, and the eternal question: Is it ever ok to bring your own seasonings to restaurants?

AI agents? I have reservations

This week’s addition to the AI hellscape? Personal AI agents. Meta released Muse, and Instinct continues to gain traction. These are agents that can respond to emails, book plane tickets, secure you a spot in a workout class, arrange and rearrange your calendar, and, yes, make grab that impossible-to-get dinner reservation. Hypothetically.

Using AI agents to nab tough reservations may also get you banned from reservation platforms, as one user found out this week. The way these agents work is by spamming the reservation platform hundreds of times per hour for hours on end. The reservation platforms flag that as suspicious activity, and may ban your account.

When I reached out to Resy for comment, a spokesperson clarified that the company doesn’t permit “unapproved third-party bots or AI agents to independently access or interact with the Resy platform.” That’s not to say the company is anti-AI—it’s recently announced integrations with ChatGPT and Claude. But rather, it says, Resy wants to maintain a “fair reservation experience for diners.”

And that’s really the crux of the issue; it’s not hard to imagine a day in the not-too-distant future when AI agents can work within a platform's terms of service (in fact, that day may have actually been earlier this week) grabbing the toughest tables the second they become available. It’s an undeniable upping of the ante in the already impossible reservations war. What are non-agent-assisted restaurant lovers to do? How can restaurants, many dependent on these platforms to stay booked, respond? Is this the beginning of a golden age for walk-in only spots?

What exactly makes a food ultraprocessed?

This week, California approved a landmark bill that establishes a process for which foods may label themselves as non-ultraprocessed. This comes after the state was the first in the nation to put forth a solid definition of what exactly an ultraprocessed food is. Although there’s been a lot of talk about ultraprocessed foods (or UPFs)—mostly stemming from the MAHA movement—there’s not a true consensus on how to delineate which foods are ultraprocessed and which aren’t.

I mean, sure, maybe you simply know it when you see it: an apple is not ultraprocessed. Gently glowing, fire-engine red flamin’ hot cheetos boxed mac and cheese is ultraprocessed.

At the federal level, the US is still in the process of drawing up an official definition, but around the world, several definitions are held as true. Brazilian researchers define UPFs as all foods with industrial ingredients like sweeteners or emulsifiers. Research group Healthy Eating Research says they’re foods “processed to the extent that they are no longer recognizable as their original plant/animal source.”

Though there isn’t a firm categorization (yet), we’re already beginning to see colossal food companies respond to the discourse. PepsiCo is reportedly shifting focus to fresh foods instead of processed ones, and some cereal companies have stopped using artificial dyes. All good stuff, but I will say this: You can pry my flamin’ hot cheetos mac and cheese out of my cold, dead, cholesterol-clogged hands.

Some people bring their own birthday cakes to restaurants. Others bring their own bottle of wine to enjoy with dinner. And then there are the people who bring their own seasonings to restaurants. It’s a controversial topic, but for those who don’t leave the house without their pocket Maldon, their Calabrian chili oil, their fancy olive oil it’s really no question at all. Read Maggie Hennessy’s intriguing piece on Bon Appétit for more.

items.title: How Much You Need to Exercise for Better Sleep, According to Experts
items.author: Dean Stattmann
items.summary: Ever notice how some workouts put you to sleep while others make you feel like someone switched out your vitamins for caffeine pills? You’re not going crazy.
items.text:
Ever notice how some workouts put you to sleep while others make you feel like someone switched out your vitamins for caffeine pills? You’re not going crazy. Exercise can significantly impact your sleep—for better or for worse—depending on how, and when, you work out.

Unfortunately, the exercise-sleep relationship is not as straightforward as the internet’s sleepmaxxers might lead you to believe. While research has unlocked some valuable insights that you can start putting into practice later tonight, there’s still a lot we don’t know. "Part of what's vexing about this is we don't have the mechanism totally locked down,” says James Wyatt, PhD, clinical sleep disorder specialist at Rush University System for Health in Chicago.

"It's also important to caveat that, while the data is enormously helpful, there's so much intra-individual variability,” says Kristen Holmes, PhD, global head of human performance and principal scientist at Whoop. At the end of the day (literally), sleep is a complex chemical equation that differs to various degrees from person to person.

But back to those valuable insights. From morning HIIT workouts that reset your circadian rhythm to an evening workout to hack your body’s natural cooling system, here are some of the best ways to use exercise to fall asleep faster, according to experts.

Working out in general won’t make you fall asleep faster

Exercise can certainly reduce the time it takes to fall asleep, but not for the reason that many wellness influencers would have you think—that is, by spurring your body’s natural production of adenosine, a sleep-inducing compound that is also a byproduct of exercise.

Your body’s cells rely on a molecule called adenosine triphosphate, or ATP, for energy. It’s a universal fuel source that powers everything from muscle contractions to brain function to simply existing. As ATP is utilized, it produces a compound called adenosine. Adenosine is not a waste product. In fact, it is highly valuable. “In muscle, adenosine helps to reduce inflammation and limit damage during periods of metabolic stress,” says Dr. Holmes. Meanwhile, in the brain, adenosine accumulates throughout the day, gradually making you feel sleepier. “In sleep science, this is called ‘sleep pressure,’” says Dr. Holmes.

So it seems perfectly plausible that the key to falling asleep faster would simply be to exercise. More exertion equals more adenosine and therefore greater sleep pressure. A 2007 study published in the journal Neuroscience actually found that when rats engaged in intense exercise, the levels of adenosine in their brains increased significantly.

But that’s not how it works in humans. "Adenosine can do an awful lot of different things in the brain and in the body, but we have to separate these,” says Dr. Wyatt. This is because adenosine doesn’t cross the blood-brain barrier—the wrapping around your brain that selectively allows certain chemicals in and not others. “If you build up adenosine in your body as a byproduct of exercising, that will not influence what happens in your brain,” Dr. Wyatt says. “That adenosine doesn't make it into the brain.”

Make no mistake, adenosine is still crucial for sleep in humans. "Adenosine on its own is one of the major chemicals that helps us fall asleep at night and get deep sleep for the first couple of hours,” Dr. Wyatt says. But only adenosine that is created in the brain will ultimately contribute to increasing sleep pressure.

The timing of your workout may be more important than the intensity

In terms of how hard or you need to work out in order to fall asleep faster, experts aren’t entirely sure of this, or if it even matters all that much. "We don't have a lot of great data on the intensity of exercise that's needed,” says Dr. Wyatt. The main reason for this, it seems, is that exercise’s ability to improve sleep is likely not a direct function of intensity—or any single factor, for that matter—but rather a combination of variables, including timing. For example, working out at a high intensity could be helpful in the morning, but detrimental later on in the day.

"One way that exercise could indirectly influence sleep is that it strengthens your circadian rhythm—that 24-hour daily rhythm of alertness during the day and sleepiness at night,” says Dr. Wyatt. In other words, working out earlier in the day can help your body understand that it’s daytime, and that in a couple of hours it will be time to sleep. But slow cardio isn’t going to cut it. “In animals, if you look at a rat or a mouse, the time during the day when you give them access to exercise dramatically shifts their circadian rhythm,” Dr. Wyatt says. “But in humans, exercise is a very weak signal for aligning ourselves to the 24-hour day, so it has to be an awful lot of exercise to have a notable effect.” (We recommend giving this HIIT workout a try.)

As for going all out in the evening, in a 2025 study published in the journal Nature Communications, researchers observed that high-strain workouts done within four hours of bedtime had a range of detrimental effects on sleep. In the study, data from nearly 15,000 Whoop members across more than four million nights revealed that an intense evening workout can delay sleep onset, reduce total sleep duration, and degrade overall sleep quality. “Basically, what we found is that intense exercise ending within four hours of going to bed was associated with these changes in sleep,” says Dr. Holmes. “When you're exercising at a high intensity, you're releasing adrenaline, cortisol, and epinephrine, so it's going to take time afterwards for that to dissipate.”

How to work out to fall asleep faster

According to Dr. Wyatt and Dr. Holmes, there are basically two types of workouts that may potentially help you fall asleep faster. The first one, as mentioned, is a high-intensity session during the day—the earlier the better—to help click your circadian rhythm into sync with the day. Ideally, you’ll want to also include some natural sunlight in the equation or, better yet, train outdoors. “From a circadian perspective, you want to create as much contrast between the day and the night as possible,” says Dr. Holmes.

The other option is an evening workout—albeit a relatively light one. According to the Whoop study data, when people engaged in a low-intensity evening workout, they experienced better sleep quality than those who didn’t exercise at all—and they only needed one hour of buffer time between training and going to bed.

The sleep-inducing power of a low-intensity evening workout has nothing to do with your circadian rhythm and everything to do with body temperature. As you approach bedtime, your body is naturally configured to move heat away from its core—a process that contributes to feelings of sleepiness. Exercise, of course, does the opposite and raises your core temperature, but it also makes your body work harder to lower it. According to John Hopkins Medicine, core temperature starts to fall about 30–90 minutes after exercising. Timing your workout to end 1–2 hours before bedtime—which, according to Dr. Wyatt, also happens to be right around the time your brain starts releasing melatonin—effectively layers that post-workout temperature drop on top of your body’s natural cooling process, creating the perfect sleep storm. “Exercise ramps up body temperature even more, and therefore it has an even steeper drop,” Dr. Wyatt says. “The steepness of that drop in body temperature is what might be associated with the ability to fall asleep faster.”

“The general guidance is: Evening exercise can help sleep, too close to bed is bad, and too far away from bedtime may be ineffective. But again, there are those individual differences,” Dr. Wyatt says. “This is why it's challenging. It's not going to be just a single recipe that says, ‘Okay, do this one thing and sleep suddenly gets better.’ You have to find the combination that works for you.”

Timing your workout to end 1–2 hours before bedtime—which, according to Dr. Wyatt, also happens to be right around the time your brain starts releasing melatonin—effectively layers that post-workout temperature drop on top of your body’s natural cooling process, creating the perfect sleep storm. “Exercise ramps up body temperature even more, and therefore it has an even steeper drop,” Dr. Wyatt says. “The steepness of that drop in body temperature is what might be associated with the ability to fall asleep faster.”

“The general guidance is: Evening exercise can help sleep, too close to bed is bad, and too far away from bedtime may be ineffective. But again, there are those individual differences,” Dr. Wyatt says. “This is why it's challenging. It's not going to be just a single recipe that says, ‘Okay, do this one thing and sleep suddenly gets better.’ You have to find the combination that works for you.”

items.title: Fukushima’s Old Farming Rituals Come to Life in Haga Hideo’s Photography
items.summary: During the 1950s the photographer Haga Hideo captured traditional folk festivals in Fukushima Prefecture. Now the memories in his work have come back home,
items.text:
During the 1950s the photographer Haga Hideo captured traditional folk festivals in Fukushima Prefecture. Now the memories in his work have come back home, with the presentation of his photographic data to locals who are already putting it to work to bring these traditions back to life.

Worshipping Tanokami: The Deity of Abundant Harvests

Before becoming a professional photographer, the pioneering folklore photographer Haga Hideo (1921–2022) worked as a translator at a news agency. That career came to an end in 1952 when the agency disbanded. For a change of scene, he headed to Fukushima Prefecture, where his father was from. While staying with relatives in what is now the city of Iwaki, he encountered a New Year ritual performed among farming families.

Prior to Japan’s rapid economic development in the years after World War II, folk beliefs in the tanokami rice deity were alive and well in many parts of the country. In Fukushima, the family patriarch and his eldest son would gather the straw from the rice harvested the previous fall to create a yorishiro, an object to beckon a deity, to welcome Shōgatsu-sama, the spirit thought to bring bountiful crops. In spring, this spirit would reappear in the rice paddies to make the rice ripen; it would then leave after the fall harvest, returning to the mountains where it dwelled.

The idea of an invisible deity responsible for the bounty of nature inspired Haga, who turned his camera lens to deity-welcoming ceremonies and their carefully crafted ritual implements and offerings. Casting a closer eye on this unadorned spiritual culture, he was reminded of marebito, the concept of a divine spirit visiting from the “other world” that he had learned about from the folklorist and ethnologist Orikuchi Shinobu (1887–1953) during his university studies.

The altar for worshipping Shōgatsu-sama on the first day of the new year. (© Haga Hideo)

A ceremony to pray for a good harvest, performed after a paddy dried out during winter has been worked with a hoe in preparation for planting. (© Haga Hideo)

Preparing mochibana, bits of mochi pounded rice threaded onto branches, as a stand-in for Shōgatsu-sama, on January 13. (© Haga Hideo)

A divination ritual conducted on the evening of January 14. Twelve soybeans are roasted in the irori sunken hearth and used to predict the weather for the coming year according to the degree of charring. (© Haga Hideo)

Torigoya is conducted even today on koshōgatsu, January 15. Bamboo, straw, and New Year decorations are burned to return Shōgatsu-sama to the heavens. (© Haga Hideo)

Warmed by hearty oden stew, children gather in a hut to sing a song to drive away birds, which eat the grain the fields, in the hope of an abundant harvest. (© Haga Hideo)

Passing On the Traditions of Iwaki

In the foreword to Tanokami: Nihon no inasaku girei (Deity of the Rice Paddies: The Rice Cultivation Rituals of Japan), Haga’s first collection of photos taken in Iwaki, he explained why he had chosen to pursue this work there.

For 2,000 years, the Japanese people have grown rice, around which the belief in tanokami and associated rituals has developed. Many Japanese customs and myths have been influenced by tanokami, providing insight into how rice cultivation rituals are reflected in daily life and social structures . . . Today, modern science has made good harvests possible without the intervention of tanokami. Progress in agricultural technology and the modernization of farm life are rapidly eroding traditional village society, in which religious beliefs, crop production, and entertainment were intertwined. This is a last opportunity to record the rituals associated with rice production for posterity.

As Haga had foreseen, the rituals around rice growing were rapidly becoming simplified or had disappeared altogether. Meanwhile, the significance of rites centering around tanokami, such as Hiroshima Prefecture’s Mibu no Hana Taue and Ishikawa Prefecture’s Oku-Noto Aenokoto, has been recognized with their collective inscription by UNESCO as Intangible Cultural Heritage. Haga, who made recording folklore for posterity his lifework, passed away in 2022 at the age of 101.

Iwaki, where Haga got his start as a folklore photographer, is today on the verge of losing its traditional farming culture. The Iwaki City Museum of Folklore and Traditional Housing, which opened in 1999, is leading efforts to preserve what is left of those traditions. The museum collects and displays all manner of artifacts related to local life.

Five traditional thatched-roof houses, dismantled and transported from various parts of Iwaki, have been re-erected in the museum’s vast grounds. Meticulously preserved, they reproduce a premodern farm village. On display inside the houses are farming tools of the era; visitors can also try their hand at working in the fields and paddies outside. Iwaki schoolchildren visit here as part of their social studies lessons, and on weekends, adults can participate in workshops to learn about the local culture.

The permanent exhibit showcases farm life from the Edo period (1603–1868) to the present. (© Uzawa Akihiko)

Farm tools and artifacts, including a life-sized figure (at left) created to protect the village from evil, have been collected from various parts of Iwaki. (© Uzawa Akihiko)

A traditional home from the latter half of the nineteenth century stands in the park. (© Uzawa Akihiko)

The interior is mostly untouched. (© Uzawa Akihiko)

Mochibana prepared by children are displayed. (© Uzawa Akihiko)

Top: The Jangara Nenbutsu Odori folk entertainment performed during the midsummer bon period. Bottom: A child is taught how to make a New Year decoration. (Courtesy Iwaki City Museum of Folklore and Traditional Housing)

In the summer of 2026, Haga’s son Haga Hinata visited the folklore museum to donate 46 film rolls’ worth of digitalized photo data, to help teach local history. Sorting through the collection, the museum selected photos of folklore entertainment that had died out more than 30 years before, including them in a special exhibit during the summer.

According to curator Ōta Yūhi, “Photos depicting farming in Iwaki in the postwar years are very rare, and they are invaluable for scholarly research. For example, the folklorist Seki Keigo [1899–1990] remarked that he had understood narikizeme, the act of hitting a fruit tree with a knife to cast a spell to ensure a bountiful crop, from a written description, but that Haga’s photo was the first time he had actually seen the action performed.”

A special exhibit planned for the fall on the theme of “straw” features donated photos illustrating Shōgatsu-sama, torigoya, and other traditions. The photos will also be used for school lectures by outside speakers and are included in the Iwaki Digital Museum showcasing cultural resources. Haga says “I’m very happy that the folklore museum values local folklore and that I was able to entrust it with my father’s photos.”

Top: Haga Hinata, at right, presents digitalized photo data to museum director Yajima Noriyuki. Below: The Folk Entertainment of Iwaki exhibition, which runs until September 27, includes photos taken in 1960. (© Uzawa Akihiko)

Although acreage under cultivation has decreased, rice-growing continues. The photo at top (© Haga Hideo) shows the hamlet of Kamikamado, where Haga photographed New Year ceremonies in 1953; below (© Uzawa Akihiko) is the same setting today.

Rich Folklore Traditions Live On

Haga also called on the Fukushima Museum in Aizu-Wakamatsu to donate the digitalized contents of 138 rolls of film containing photos taken throughout the prefecture. His father’s photos had been included in an exhibition that traveled to Beijing and Rome in 2012, the year after the Great East Japan Earthquake. Haga’s presentation took place on the occasion of the return of the exhibition to the Fukushima Museum.

At the ceremony, Ōsato Masaki, the museum’s curator in charge of folklore, displayed the actual ritual implements and crafts that the photos had recorded. He explained: “Along with actual physical examples, photos are vital for explaining traditional rituals. Haga Hideo’s photos, especially those in which he focused on capturing the essence of those rituals, are priceless.”

In addition, several film strips were digitalized in chronological order, giving a good idea of the sequence of events taking place. The 1960 photos showing festivities in the town of Miharu are particularly interesting.

One sequence shows the moment a bride enters the groom’s home, a once-in-a-lifetime occasion. According to Ōsato, “Haga must have negotiated beforehand with the family, since he took photos from inside the home.” He expressed surprise that the sequence of photos “shows the go-between and a female neighbor removing the bride’s umbrellalike wicker headgear and guests chanting the celebratory ‘Takasago’ song from the nō play of the same name. These are the kinds of photos depicting a ceremony that one might expect to see in school textbooks on folklore.”

A photo from the wedding. Haga recorded the entire proceedings, from the exchange of yuinō betrothal gifts to reporting the marriage to the local shrine’s tutelary deity. (© Haga Hideo)

Top: A Fukushima Museum display of folk implements similar to those depicted in the donated photo collection. Bottom: Museum director Matsuyama Masayuki, at left, expresses pleasure at receiving the collection, which he considers a valuable resource for communicating Fukushima’s past way of life. (© Nippon.com)

Presenting the collection, Haga said, “Fukushima’s festivals are an important element in human relations. They haven’t really been in the public eye since the March 2011 earthquake, but I hope that these photos will make local people proud of their folk culture.”

A similar collection of digitalized photos, taken in the 1950s, was gifted to Kagoshima Prefecture’s Amami Ōshima in the summer of 2025; activities relating to the collection have been ongoing there. The Amami Museum held an exhibit commemorating the donation of the photos this summer and is also planning a traveling exhibition to other parts of Japan, starting with Kobe, targeting former residents of Okinoerabujima, one of the Amami islands. Perhaps a similar activity can be organized in Fukushima to communicate the local culture to younger generations.

The Kohata no Hata Matsuri in Nihonmatsu, where a coming-of-age rite for 15-year-olds includes transiting through a narrow passage to symbolically “emerge” into adulthood, is still conducted today. (© Haga Hideo)

A traditional rite in the town of Asakawa, held to protect fields and paddies from strong winds, celebrates a deity known as Kazebukuro-sama. (© Haga Hideo)

Artisans making traditional handcraft Aizu erōsoku candles. (© Haga Hideo)
