items.text:
On a cold winter night in Ketchum, Idaho, Chicago Stars midfielder Bea Franklin was pulling off a different sort of physical feat than what she usually does on the soccer field. Under the eyes of taxidermied animals at the Pioneer Saloon, she deftly balanced martinis as a cocktail waitress, wearing cowgirl boots and ensuring the olives didn’t drip when she walked down stairs.

Franklin did not take a second job as a cocktail waitress in a Rocky Mountain ski resort town not out of necessity, but as a way to think about more than just the sport that has dominated much of her life.

“It was just so much fun, and a really great way to kind of disconnect from soccer,” Franklin said.

Hardly half a decade ago, a player like Franklin, a 25-year-old in her third pro season, might have needed a job like this just to get by.

Five years ago this summer, NWSL players organized the “No More Side Hustles” campaign to highlight the league’s low pay and the need for players to get second jobs while playing, training and working as full-time professional athletes.

At the time, a third of the NWSL Players Association’s members made the league minimum salary of $22,000; 75% made $31,000 or less. Jessica McDonald, a World Cup winner, worked at Amazon packing boxes for 10 hours a day while running training sessions for young players at night. Kristen Hamilton, a three-time league champion, drove for DoorDash. Others cleaned homes, worked as receptionists or mopped floors.

It spoke to a major problem that the league has, by and large, addressed successfully. The NWSLPA agreed to its first collective bargaining agreement with the league in 2022. Under the current CBA, reached in 2024, the minimum salary for players is $50,500 for the 2026 season – nearly the same amount as the maximum in 2021 ($52,500).

Now, with the security of a living wage, players are free to take on academic, professional and entrepreneurial pursuits. Not because they have to, but because they want to.

Washington Spirit defender Gabrielle Carle is working on becoming a doctor after her playing career wraps. She said she briefly considered doing both until realizing that was too ambitious, even for her.

“I was like, ‘Oh, this is gonna be complicated,’” Carle said. “These two don’t really work together.”

items.text:
A big week for

The league phase has been previewed as Barcelona’s first step toward reclaiming a crown last lifted in 2015, with disappointments aplenty since. Lionel Messi claiming just one Champions League title in the last decade of his time at Camp Nou is the starkest statistic. The player anointed as Messi’s successor, Lamine Yamal, is already a European and world champion for Spain, so this is the next frontier. A soggy Wednesday evening at Camp Nou saw Hansi Flick’s team show their attacking chops remain of the highest quality in a 5-1 defeat of Feyenoord. The club presidential regime of Joan Laporta continues to pull levers to confound financial experts, with Gabriel Jesus, one of the summer’s arrivals, scoring his first Barca goal. Yamal got on the scoresheet via a scruffy free-kick after Raphinha had reminded there are further dimensions to that all-star attack, his first goal of his pair two sending Feyenoord defenders skidding.

Until Troy Parrott headed to Seville this summer, the chances of Real Betis v Lille being a leading attraction to the Irish diaspora were minimal. But now the team in green and white have become an Irish obsession. The goalscorer in their World Cup playoff win in Hungary last year is approaching national hero status. Opting for Andalusia instead of leading West Ham in the Championship confirmed him as a player with broad horizons; the former Tottenham trainee is hitting the heights in La Liga. Having scored the winner against Real Madrid last weekend, throwing back to José Mourinho his rejection when a Spurs teenager, he delivered again in northern France. His dragged, left-footed finish grabbed a 3-2 lead Betis successfully held. “I don’t think I’ll ever have a better night in my whole life,” Parrott said of his glory night in Budapest. If that still holds true, his Friday and Tuesday will have gone close to emulating it.

Weird scenes after Fenerbahce’s 1-1 draw with Roma when Ismail Kartal, the Turkish club’s veteran coach, resigned post-match “to clear the way”. The drama was heightened when the Fenerbahce president, Aziz Yildirim, said he would not be accepting the resignation. “There’s no need for him ‌to say that he’d continue,” Yildirim said. “I am his senior, I told him to continue and that’s it. We are a family.” The explanation given for such a sudden exit was Kartal’s annoyance at a bottle being lobbed in his direction. Watch this space.

Player of the week

Ballon D’Or season is upon us, and a leading nominee must be Bayern’s brilliant Michael Olise, who scored two goals against Bodø/Glimt. The Norwegians attempted to aggressively mark him but were left with twisted blood as his team scored five second-half goals. The Frenchman gave a typically dry post-match interview. Asked how it feels to score great goals, he said: “I don’t know … I just shoot and it goes in.”

Club in focus

Manchester United on Thursday faced a club formed in 2017, three years after Luke Shaw, who missed the game, was signed. Sabah, Azerbaijan’s champions last season, breaking the dominance of Qurban Qurbanov’s Qarabag, are coached by Valdas Dambrauskas, a former United soccer schools and Brentford youth coach who also worked as a pub cleaner and gardener in the UK. His journey from Lithuania to Manchester was funded by a win on Who Wants To Be A Millionaire, where he walked away from Vilnius’s equivalent of Regis Philbin with a sum commensurate with a year’s salary. The homecoming was not too happy as United were ready 4-0 winners, Youri Tielemans and Bruno Fernandes in particular turning on the style. “He absolutely destroyed us,” Dambrauskas said of Fernandes. That did not bode well for Sabah’s matches ahead: Dortmund, Barcelona and Napoli travel to Azerbaijan, while a trip to Arsenal awaits.

They said it

“There’s a lot of criticism when a match is boring, but it was crazy today. . … It could easily have ended 7-6. Our midfield was weak, they made changes very early, and I didn’t have much to work with in the centre of the pitch. … I agree with Raul that the goals came as a result of their errors.” José Mourinho’s Real Madrid return is already under scrutiny, and before being interviewed on Movistar after a close-run 2-1 defeat of Inter, he had to listen to on-air criticism from Raúl González, a Madrileno legend. Those midfield comments appeared directed at Trent Alexander-Arnold, who played as one of the trio on a night where fans at the Santiago Bernabéu made clear that better is expected.

The other side of an elongated international break, the wait will be long – more than a month – for the second round of matches. Holders Paris Saint-Germain, looking for their third straight title, travelling to Manchester City is the grand-slam fixture. Enzo Maresca has made a decent fist of succeeding Pep Guardiola, with four wins in four. items.author: Jacob Steinberg
items.summary: Premier League representation is low when it comes to the 16 attacking players on this year’s Ballon d’Or shortlist. Manchester United’s Bruno Fernandes and
items.text:
Premier League representation is low when it comes to the 16 attacking players on this year’s Ballon d’Or shortlist. Manchester United’s Bruno Fernandes and Manchester City’s Erling Haaland are there but Cole Palmer, one of the nominees in 2025, is out after an injury-hit year and English football’s shift towards physicality and set pieces last season is summed up by none of the forwards from the best team in the country making the cut.

The trio giving Arsenal a presence – Gabriel Maghalhães, Declan Rice and William Saliba – are all defensive minded. Arsenal won the league but their forwards are not regarded as elite. Injuries played a part, denying Martin Ødegaard, Kai Havertz and Bukayo Saka fluency, but Mikel Arteta’s side were not loved by neutrals. There was respect rather than admiration for their defensive rigour. There was an argument that a lack of ambition after going 1-0 up stopped Arsenal from beating Paris Saint-Germain in the Champions League final.

It was a close-run thing, but a second consecutive European title for PSG was a victory for attacking football over the Premier League’s attrition. Luis Enrique’s side keep beating English opponents, and there was a similar vibe at the World Cup. Games flowed more in North America, in part because of officials clamping down on the “meat wall” at set pieces.

As for England, Thomas Tuchel’s plan to tap into the Premier League’s physicality failed. England retreated in their semi-final defeat by Argentina. It is also significant that not until Anthony Gordon’s goal against Argentina did an England attacker who played in the Premier League last season score at the World Cup.

“Spanish football demands a different level of tactical and technical intelligence,” Gordon has said since leaving Newcastle for Barcelona. “In England, sometimes intensity can cover up mistakes. You can miscontrol the ball and still recover by winning the next physical battle.”

The English top flight’s appeal partly rests on those bruising qualities but the grind went too far last season. How many classic games can you remember? Some of the top sides having disappointing campaigns did not help but across the board there was grumbling about an over-reliance on set pieces and goalkeepers being squashed during elaborate corner routines. Anthony Barry, Tuchel’s assistant, noted that the game had become congealed in the middle. There was an emphasis on long throws and timewasting. The league was harder to watch.

Now comes the shift. One of the themes during the first three weeks of the campaign has been the pace quickening. Lawmakers have reacted. The five-second countdown and threat of a restart reversal at goalkicks and throw-ins have forced teams to think twice about timewasting. The 10-second time limit on players leaving the pitch at substitutions has helped and a trial with tactical timeouts mean an outfield player will have to go off for at least a minute after the restart of play if their side’s goalkeeper has gone down injured.

Early days, of course, but the football has been enjoyable and the numbers are encouraging. There have been four matches in which both teams have had 14 shots this season, compared with only one at the same stage last year. According to Opta, the average ball-in-play time has increased from 55min 23sec during the 2025-26 campaign to 57min 14sec. Delay times are down from 29.2sec to 26.7sec. Excluding penalties, the percentage of goals from set pieces has dipped from 27.5% to 23.5%.

Graphic showing Premier League games have been more end-to-end early in 2026‑27

There are more fast breaks per game (2.27 compared with 1.94), more shots per game via fast breaks (1.9 compared with 1.75) and more goals from fast breaks per game (0.43 from 0.23). Chelsea, more transitional under Xabi Alonso, are flowing and have been involved in some wild games. Liverpool have replaced Arne Slot with the counterpressing Andoni Iraola. Newcastle have been rapid under Matthias Jaissle, who has played to the strengths of Harvey Barnes and Anthony Elanga. Roberto De Zerbi seems an outlier at Tottenham, who need to speed up. Manchester City may soon want more incision from Enzo Maresca. The Italian favours a methodical style but even Pep Guardiola was moving away from obsessive control last season. There is a sense that some managers are closer in style to Jürgen Klopp than Guardiola at the moment. Alonso’s style has seemed very similar to Klopp so far. His willingness to let talent breathe is also quite like Carlo Ancelotti; Palmer has spoken about being allowed more freedom to roam under Alonso.

Perhaps there will be a correction as teams wise up to each other, Europe kicks in and injuries bite. Perhaps it will amuse you to hear that Arsenal remain top for delaying at a corner (with an average of 43.2sec). Then again, last Sunday delivered the season’s first clash between potential title rivals – Arsenal taking on Chelsea at the Emirates Stadium – and the action was breathless. Chelsea did not hold back and it was interesting that Arsenal welcomed the end-to-end openness.

Havertz was full of imagination up front and Ødegaard, Arsenal’s creative hub, dominated. It is a fascinating development. Defence was Arsenal’s greatest asset last season; Rice was more influential than Ødegaard in midfield. Now the Norwegian looks rejuvenated. Fitness helps but so does greater freedom. Chelsea did not shut the game down, so Ødegaard ran it. The best player in the best team was not a defender. At those levels Ødegaard looks as good as Fernandes.

This matters. Florian Wirtz, a star in Alonso’s champion Bayer Leverkusen side, has come to England and found the pace difficult at Liverpool. The Premier League needs top talent to feel it can shine. The three Bayern Munich forwards on the Ballon d’Or shortlist – Harry Kane, Luis Díaz and Michael Olise – moved from English teams. PSG’s Ousmane Dembélé and Khvicha Kvaratskhelia are fresh for the business end of the Champions League in part because they aren’t being pushed to the limit by teams such as Brentford and Bournemouth on the weekend. Jude Bellingham, England’s jewel, has never played in the Premier League. Vinícius Júnior toyed with moving to Arsenal but stayed with Kylian Mbappé at Real Madrid.

The Premier League is the strongest and most competitive in Europe. Yet there has been a talent drain. It is easy to imagine the best forwards feel they will have more fun creating and scoring against less intense Bundesliga defences and have the freshness to compete for the Champions League, international tournaments and for individual prizes.

Look at how the four semi-finalists at the World Cup were well represented by Premier League defenders and defensive midfielders but not by wingers and strikers. Where are the stars? Those who have left have mostly not been replaced, which is why the Premier League could do with Bradley Barcola shining at Liverpool after his arrival from PSG.

Barcola succeeding could convince others to follow. If the France winger is worn down, though, it could have the opposite effect. The Premier League has to be careful. The new measures to tackle timewasting could be a gamechanger. There were only four added minutes at the end of each half when Arsenal beat Chelsea. It felt refreshing.

There was an argument that a lack of ambition after going 1-0 up stopped Arsenal from beating Paris Saint-Germain in the Champions League final.

It was a close-run thing, but a second consecutive European title for PSG was a victory for attacking football over the Premier League’s attrition. Luis Enrique’s side keep beating English opponents, and there was a similar vibe at the World Cup. Games flowed more in North America, in part because of officials clamping down on the “meat wall” at set pieces.

As for England, Thomas Tuchel’s plan to tap into the Premier League’s physicality failed. England retreated in their semi-final defeat by Argentina. It is also significant that not until Anthony Gordon’s goal against Argentina did an England attacker who played in the Premier League last season score at the World Cup.

“Spanish football demands a different level of tactical and technical intelligence,” Gordon has said since leaving Newcastle for Barcelona. “In England, sometimes intensity can cover up mistakes. You can miscontrol the ball and still recover by winning the next physical battle.”

The English top flight’s appeal partly rests on those bruising qualities but the grind went too far last season. How many classic games can you remember? Some of the top sides having disappointing campaigns did not help but across the board there was grumbling about an over-reliance on set pieces and goalkeepers being squashed during elaborate corner routines. Anthony Barry, Tuchel’s assistant, noted that the game had become congealed in the middle. There was an emphasis on long throws and timewasting. The league was harder to watch.
https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/ff61379a2f1cf06ebcc12bb42e34381031460d28/0_0_7119_4747/master/7119.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none

blocks.x: Now comes the shift. One of the themes during the first three weeks of the campaign has been the pace quickening. Lawmakers have reacted. The five-second countdown and threat of a restart reversal at goalkicks and throw-ins have forced teams to think twice about timewasting. The 10-second time limit on players leaving the pitch at substitutions has helped and a trial with tactical timeouts mean an outfield player will have to go off for at least a minute after the restart of play if their side’s goalkeeper has gone down injured.

Early days, of course, but the football has been enjoyable and the numbers are encouraging. There have been four matches in which both teams have had 14 shots this season, compared with only one at the same stage last year. According to Opta, the average ball-in-play time has increased from 55min 23sec during the 2025-26 campaign to 57min 14sec. Delay times are down from 29.2sec to 26.7sec. Excluding penalties, the percentage of goals from set pieces has dipped from 27.5% to 23.5%.
Graphic showing Premier League games have been more end-to-end early in 2026‑27

There are more fast breaks per game (2.27 compared with 1.94), more shots per game via fast breaks (1.9 compared with 1.75) and more goals from fast breaks per game (0.43 from 0.23). Chelsea, more transitional under Xabi Alonso, are flowing and have been involved in some wild games. Liverpool have replaced Arne Slot with the counterpressing Andoni Iraola. Newcastle have been rapid under Matthias Jaissle, who has played to the strengths of Harvey Barnes and Anthony Elanga. Roberto De Zerbi seems an outlier at Tottenham, who need to speed up. Manchester City may soon want more incision from Enzo Maresca. The Italian favours a methodical style but even Pep Guardiola was moving away from obsessive control last season. There is a sense that some managers are closer in style to Jürgen Klopp than Guardiola at the moment. Alonso’s style has seemed very similar to Klopp so far. His willingness to let talent breathe is also quite like Carlo Ancelotti; Palmer has spoken about being allowed more freedom to roam under Alonso.

blocks.c: Chelsea's Cole Palmer, Liverpool's Bradley Barcola, Arsenal's Kai Havertz.

blocks.x: Perhaps there will be a correction as teams wise up to each other, Europe kicks in and injuries bite. Perhaps it will amuse you to hear that Arsenal remain top for delaying at a corner (with an average of 43.2sec). Then again, last Sunday delivered the season’s first clash between potential title rivals – Arsenal taking on Chelsea at the Emirates Stadium – and the action was breathless. Chelsea did not hold back and it was interesting that Arsenal welcomed the end-to-end openness.

skip past newsletter promotion

Havertz was full of imagination up front and Ødegaard, Arsenal’s creative hub, dominated. It is a fascinating development. Defence was Arsenal’s greatest asset last season; Rice was more influential than Ødegaard in midfield. Now the Norwegian looks rejuvenated. Fitness helps but so does greater freedom. Chelsea did not shut the game down, so Ødegaard ran it. The best player in the best team was not a defender. At those levels Ødegaard looks as good as Fernandes.
https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/451767014729cbded293cce26769c53dc1cd1d26/0_0_3703_2469/master/3703.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none

blocks.x: This matters. Florian Wirtz, a star in Alonso’s champion Bayer Leverkusen side, has come to England and found the pace difficult at Liverpool. The Premier League needs top talent to feel it can shine. The three Bayern Munich forwards on the Ballon d’Or shortlist – Harry Kane, Luis Díaz and Michael Olise – moved from English teams. PSG’s Ousmane Dembélé and Khvicha Kvaratskhelia are fresh for the business end of the Champions League in part because they aren’t being pushed to the limit by teams such as Brentford and Bournemouth on the weekend. Jude Bellingham, England’s jewel, has never played in the Premier League. Vinícius Júnior toyed with moving to Arsenal but stayed with Kylian Mbappé at Real Madrid.

The Premier League is the strongest and most competitive in Europe. Yet there has been a talent drain. It is easy to imagine the best forwards feel they will have more fun creating and scoring against less intense Bundesliga defences and have the freshness to compete for the Champions League, international tournaments and for individual prizes.

Look at how the four semi-finalists at the World Cup were well represented by Premier League defenders and defensive midfielders but not by wingers and strikers. Where are the stars? Those who have left have mostly not been replaced, which is why the Premier League could do with Bradley Barcola shining at Liverpool after his arrival from PSG.

Barcola succeeding could convince others to follow. If the France winger is worn down, though, it could have the opposite effect. The Premier League has to be careful. The new measures to tackle timewasting could be a gamechanger. There were only four added minutes at the end of each half when Arsenal beat Chelsea. It felt refreshing.

items.text:
Saturday

Golf

6.40am (all times BST)Solheim Cup live

The 20th edition of the Solheim Cup is under way, and for the first time in the Netherlands. Angela Stanford’s Americans are the slight favourites and defending champions, but they have not won on European soil since Germany in 2015. The US, as holders, need only 14 of the 28 points available to retain the crystal trophy. Scott Murray and Matt Cooper offer live coverage of day two’s foursomes (6.40am) and fourballs (12.05am), with Ewan Murray reporting from Bernardus Golf.

Football

8amMatchday live

Join Tom Bassam for the latest news and buildup to Saturday’s football action. We will keep pace with all the day’s breaking news from around the grounds for seven Premier League matches, plus a full Championship and EFL programme. Join our Matchday live community by sending your thoughts and queries to matchday.live@theguardian.com.

Premier League

3pmClockwatch

Barry Glendenning keeps watch over all five 3pm kick-offs in the Premier League, and will be focusing on two of the afternoon’s most compelling games. Liverpool’s season took ⁠a while to get going under Andoni Iraola but after wins at Ipswich and then Atlético Madrid in the Champions League they will relish another home clash against a Fulham side managed by the former Liverpool player Álvaro Arbeloa. After three successive defeats and seven goals conceded, Arbeloa is already feeling the pressure of management in the top flight. Alongside last season’s top two, only promoted Hull remain unbeaten but their brilliant start faces an acid test against Xabi Alonso’s free-scoring Chelsea.

Formula One

3pmSpanish Grand Prix qualifying live

Kimi Antonelli is Formula One’s man of the moment but Mercedes’ 20-year-old championship leader faces a Monumental challenge in Spain this weekend, along with all his rivals. Fresh from ⁠becoming the first Italian since ⁠1966 to win his home race at Monza, Antonelli will be entering new territory when the Spanish capital’s Madring makes its grand prix debut with its signature La Monumental. The banked curve is a 550m-long high-speed 270-degree bend with a crest on the exit meaning drivers momentarily take it blind as they look up at the sky. Mercedes, winners of nine ‌of the first 13 races, should be in the mix but can expect a tougher fight than Monza, where they finished one-two, putting Antonelli 66 points clear of ‌his teammate George Russell. We will have lap-by-lap coverage of qualifying from Philip Cornwall, and Giles Richards reporting from Madrid.

Premier League

5.30pmTottenham v Everton live

Despite a £300m close-season splurge, Roberto De Zerbi’s Spurs are winless in their first three games and without a goal. Little more than three months ago, the Italian completed his Tottenham rescue mission as they beat Everton on the final day of the season to secure their top-flight status. On Saturday, David Moyes’ Everton are the visitors again and, while the stakes are not so high, De Zerbi desperately needs a victory to instil some belief that the money has been well spent. There will be a live blog of the match, with David Hytner reporting from Tottenham Hotspur Stadium.

Tennis

7pmUS Open women’s singles final

Elena Rybakina rallied to beat Coco Gauff in a thrilling semi-final to earn a title showdown with the defending champion, Aryna Sabalenka, and take a step towards her third grand slam crown. The pair have met in two previous slam finals, with Sabalenka defeating Rybakina in the 2023 Australian Open decider before the second seed ​levelled the score at Melbourne Park in ‌January. Sabalenka, who will lose her world No 1 status to her opponent on Monday regardless of the result, is seeking to join Chris Evert and Serena Williams as the only women to win three straight US Open titles. Katy Murrells helms the live blog, with Tumaini Carayol reporting from Flushing Meadows.

Premier League

8pmSunderland v Arsenal live

Stability has been the order of the day at Arsenal, with Mikel Arteta’s side straight back into last term’s groove. Arsenal visit Sunderland, a fixture they will be wary of after being held to a 2-2 draw at the Stadium of Light last season. The Gunners made it four wins from four with a 1-0 victory at Napoli in their Champions League opener on Wednesday night and – with three victories in the Premier League already under their belt – show no signs of faltering. Billy Munday liveblogs the match and Louise Taylor reports.

Rugby union

10pmSouth Africa v New Zealand live

After three bruising contests, South Africa go in search of a third successive Test victory over ⁠the All Blacks that would secure the four-game series for the world champions and lay down a marker for next year’s title defence. The ⁠final game of New ⁠Zealand’s six-week, ​eight-match tour of South Africa is being played in the United States as the top-ranked sides in the world look ⁠to promote the Rugby’s Greatest Rivalry series to a wider audience at the 70,000-seater home of the NFL’s Baltimore Ravens. Daniel Gallan buckles up as blog host.

Sunday

Boxing

3amRyan Garcia v Conor Benn live

Ryan Garcia enters his WBC welterweight title fight showdown with Conor Benn carrying the belt but understanding that winning the belt and establishing himself as a legitimate champion are different accomplishments. The American captured the first recognised world title of his turbulent career in February, dominating his compatriot Mario Barrios over 12 rounds for a unanimous decision. The performance showcased a more disciplined, complete fighter than the social media phenomenon who built his reputation on blinding speed and a devastating left hook. Now he must prove that victory began a sustained championship run. His first defence comes at T-Mobile Arena in Las Vegas, where personal hostility and contrasting styles should produce a revealing test. The British fighter intends to pressure Garcia, force exchanges and make the fight physical. Bryan Armen Graham has round-by-round coverage of the big fight.

Football

8amMatchday live

Emillia Hawkins clocks on bright and early to preview Sunday’s action with breaking news and much more as we settle down for two Premier League fixtures, with all the noise around the afternoon’s Manchester derby. Email matchday.live@theguardian.com with your notions and queries.

Golf

10.10amSolheim Cup live

Scott Murray is back at post for the deciding singles contests as Europe seek to regain the trophy after losing 15½-12½ in Virginia two years ago in the biggest team event in women’s golf.

Women’s Super League

12pmManchester United v Chelsea live

Emillia Hawkins then turns to live commentary as last season’s fourth- and third-place teams respectively meet for the first time this season, both seeking a first win of the campaign. United lost to London City last weekend as Eva Olid took charge of the club for the first time in the WSL while Sonia Bompastor’s Chelsea were held by Aston Villa at Stamford Bridge despite battering the visitors with 35 shots. Suzanne Wrack reports.

Scottish League Cup quarter-final

12pmRangers v Celtic live

The Hoops’ only blemish this term remains their Champions League playoff capitulation away to Lask, and overcoming their Old Firm rivals at Ibrox to reach the semi-final of the Premier Sports Cup would help maintain their momentum. There will, however, be no Celtic fans in attendance after the recent decision not to allow away supporters at any matches between the two Glasgow giants this term to avoid the trouble that marred last season’s Scottish Cup collision. The anxiety from the Light Blues legions, which has been prevalent in some games in Govan, resurfaced on Wednesday night as the home side struggled in the Premiership match against St Mirren after missing several chances before the break. However, a pressure valve was released when Bojan Miovski scored in stoppage time for a crucial 1-0 win, making it four victories in a row for Derek McInnes and his side. Taha Hashim liveblogs the cup tie, and Paul MacInnes reports.

Formula One

2pmSpanish Grand Prix

John Brewin has lap-by-lap coverage as Formula One sweeps into Madrid for a first look at the Madring. Mercedes are in the ascendant and Kimi Antonelli can still put the equivalent of three race wins between him and Russell, with the Briton chasing a first win since Austria in June to prevent his title hopes from withering further. McLaren, who won in the Netherlands and Hungary with the reigning world champion, Lando Norris, and have Oscar Piastri hungry to open his account, could be the main rivals. Ferrari’s Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc drove the Madring when it was still a building site on a scorching filming day in July but there is an underlying tension in the camp after last weekend’s opening-lap shenanigans at Monza.

Premier League

4.30pmManchester United v Manchester City live

After all the pre-season optimism, United’s start to the season has been inconsistent but Sunday’s derby offers Michael Carrick’s side an early chance ⁠to show they are contenders. City, meanwhile, arrive at Old Trafford with a perfect record under their new manager, Enzo Maresca, although their performances have suggested there is still work to do after Pep Guardiola’s departure. Carrick’s impact at United last season as interim manager after the club’s parting of ways with Ruben Amorim in January was dramatic, beginning with a 2-0 home victory over City. Their rivals will provide an acid test, especially with Erling Haaland firing on all cylinders having scored both goals in the 2-0 win at Porto in the Champions League on Tuesday to make it five goals in three games so far this season. Rob Smyth liveblogs the big game of the weekend, with Jamie Jackson and Will Unwin reporting from Old Trafford.

Tennis

7pmUS Open men’s singles final

The men’s singles semis pitted Alexander Zverev against Karen Khachanov and Frances Tiafoe with Ben Shelton. The latter pairing are on a quest to become the first American men’s grand slam champion ⁠since Andy Roddick’s 2003 triumph at Flushing Meadows. Whoever emerges victorious will collide in Sunday evening’s final, and Ella Brockway has live blog commentary of the showdown.

items.title: Pochettino’s ‘different’ vow to the US invites unwelcome speculation
items.author: Jeff Rueter
items.summary: I hope, in this lifetime, you find someone who loves you the way Mauricio Pochettino loves Tottenham Hotspur. The grip Spurs have on his heart seems the stuff
items.text:
I hope, in this lifetime, you find someone who loves you the way Mauricio Pochettino loves Tottenham Hotspur. The grip Spurs have on his heart seems the stuff of a literary classic: his imperfect partner who called things off at the first sign of trouble must merely check in on him occasionally to rekindle hopes of a reunion.

Perhaps a bit extreme, but this week’s revelation – that he’d return to Tottenham even if they were relegated and chalking his absence up to imperfect timing, not the part about handing the club a decade-old title – has implicity laid out the terms of his return as United States manager. Others may always have interest in his services, and a certain North London suitor will never get the door slammed in their face outright.

“Now it’s a four-year contract, it’s different,” Pochettino said this week. “We can next season lose the Copa América or the Gold Cup, they’re not happy with us and they can sack us. Or we can say: ‘OK. It’s not in the way that we think.’ Four years is different. Maybe now if someone calls in the future, it’s a different, different type [of thing]. We are excited, we are thinking to spend four years to the next World Cup. But now it’s a long period.”

If you’re a Spurs fan, it warms the heart to revisit last decade’s glory days. If you’re a US fan, you’re quite sick of hearing so much about a team besides the one he’s managing. In that sense, Pochettino is among esteemed company.

In his opening press conference, he read aloud to the press his terms of service – and was celebrated for it. Carlo Ancelotti was in no rush to abandon Brazil after a middling tournament, despite real questions about the pool’s depth and quality in midfield. Even Pep Guardiola held talks with Italy immediately after his decade in Manchester.

What’s different about Pochettino from, say, Klopp is his perceived eagerness to return to the club grind. Even atop the Red Bull Football conglomerate, Klopp was quick to brush aside any insinuations about returning to management. There may be a simple answer. Each of Ancelotti, Guardiola, and Klopp – company with which Pochettino is regularly associated – has been the champion of England and Europe. Pochettino, at this stage, has not reached those summits.

Is aiming for a Copa América semi-final more enticing than restoring Tottenham to previous heights? What about reaching a World Cup quarter-final an ocean away from the tens of thousands who soundtracked the previous one? What can US Soccer offer that his caliber of clubs – Tottenham and beyond – can’t exceed?

While Pochettino and his charges have something resembling an excuse for their lack of execution against Belgium, the fact remains that the USMNT were once again eliminated in the last-16. Just like they were under Bob Bradley in 2010. And Jürgen Klinsmann in 2014. And Gregg Berhalter in 2022.

In theory, Pochettino will enter his second cycle in a position of strength having undertaken a thorough examination of the player pool. The fresh faces are no longer MLS journeymen or players in Europe’s lesser divisions. Instead, they’re promising prospects: 16-year-old wonderkid Cavan Sullivan, new Crystal Palace showman Zavier Gozo, highly anticipated La Masia netminder Diego Kochen.

If anything, working the up-and-comers into the established core and identifying sturdier central defenders to partner with Chris Richards should be an incredibly exciting project. The core is in great shape, with this summer’s headliners – Folarin Balogun, Alex Freeman, Richards, and Malik Tillman – all aged 30 or younger in the summer of 2030. There’s plenty of reason to think that the program is better positioned for a deep run at the next World Cup than the 2026.

Actualizing that potential will require a clear vision and a dedicated effort to raise this team’s standard throughout every window of the next four years. Batting eyelashes at past employers hardly projects that level of dedication. And so, for the next four years just like the past one, the biggest question surrounding the USMNT won’t be how far they can go in 2030. It’ll be whether Pochettino will still be the man leading them there.

1. Wirtz’s worth ‘not all about statistics’

Andoni Iraola has insisted Florian Wirtz should be judged by his influence on Liverpool rather than statistics and believes the player’s impact will increase as his rapport with a new-look attack develops.

Wirtz impressed in Liverpool’s defeat of Atlético Madrid on Wednesday, having also produced some of his best performances last season in the Champions League. But he has also come in for criticism this season for the amount of times he has conceded possession. The £116m Germany international has one assist and no goals in the Premier League so far.

“Flo played very well against Atlético Madrid and I also think he has been unlucky,” said Iraola. “I remember the ‘goal’ he scored against Nottingham Forest; they gave it live and then VAR disallowed it. He could have had very good assists but we haven’t finished them. That is why you cannot just play because of the numbers.

“Whether a striker scores a lot of goals or he doesn’t, you have to look at the performances. Does he help us to play well? Yes. Well, someone will score the goals and someone will give the assists. I am not too focused on numbers. Nowadays everything is about numbers, everyone tells players you have to assist, you have to score goals. For me, you have to help us play well. Someone will score the goals and I don’t care if it is the midfielders like it was the other day. Someone will score the goals if we are doing well collectively.”

Wirtz created an excellent chance for Bradley Barcola against Atlético and Iraola believes the 23-year-old will exert a greater influence as his understanding with the France international and fellow new signing Victor Muñoz improves.

“There is an argument to make that the wingers have changed more than anywhere else,” Iraola said. “Now we have new weapons we can use with Bradley and Victor. With Florian, he is key for us. I am not worried because he will quickly learn where Victor prefers the ball or where Bradley prefers the ball. And, also, Bradley in just his second game you could see they already had a good association. I am not very worried.” Andy Hunter

2. Grealish ‘can be a wingers’ role model’

David Moyes has told Jack Grealish he wants him to become a role model at Everton for fellow wingers Tyrique George and Tyler Dibling.

Grealish made an immediate impact from the bench against Manchester United last Sunday in his first outing since rejoining Everton on loan from Manchester City. Despite a lack of minutes in pre-season, as he recovered from the fractured foot that curtailed his first campaign with Everton, the 31-year-old could start for Moyes’s side at Tottenham on Saturday. The Everton manager wants Grealish to take on more responsibility this season.

“Jack knows when he comes here there is an opportunity for him to play and to show what he can do,” Moyes said. “But I also want him to be a senior professional and a role model. We’ve got Tyrique and Tyler and if ever you are looking at somebody for how to play as a wide player, Jack Grealish would certainly be one of them.

“I think both of them could learn an awful lot from Jack and I want him to become that senior citizen among them, somebody who teaches them. We’ve got a mature Jack Grealish now as well in terms of understanding the game and being a team player – not that he is an individual but he plays with an individual style.”

Moyes believes there is greater expectation on Grealish given it is his second season at the club and there is a need to fill the creative gap created by Iliman Ndiaye’s departure. “If there is one person who would be able to carry that it would be Jack, just because of the way he is,” he added.

“He will find it easy to carry expectation and he’ll be happy to do so. That’s his character. Everybody wants Jack to get back to where he was. His first three months for us last season was hugely important in getting us wins so now it is about getting him right to perform at that level again.

“He’s had six and a half months out. He’s had no pre-season games, he came on for 15 minutes in the Community Shield, so he’s had no real football and Jack is someone who thrives on the football. He gets himself fit through the games more so than the training. We need to be careful and see how he goes but he’s looking good.” Andy Hunter

3. João Pedro ‘as good as Haaland’, says Alonso

Xabi Alonso has claimed João Pedro is at Erling Haaland’s level and similar in style to Karim Benzema. The Chelsea striker has reacted to missing out on Brazil’s World Cup squad by making an excellent start to the season and was named the Premier League’s player of the month on Friday.

João Pedro has scored twice in his first three league appearances and has formed an exciting attacking trio with Cole Palmer and Morgan Rogers. Chelsea have scored 16 goals in all competitions and Alonso did not hold back when asked if the 24-year-old is as good as Haaland. “I would say yes,” Chelsea’s manager said. “If you count how many top strikers we have in the Premier League, I’m sure that João is there. Haaland for sure is there. So I would rate him that way.”

The range of João Pedro’s game has added to his threat. Alonso played with Benzema at Real Madrid and sees similarities between the pair. “In many things he reminds me of Benzema,” he said. “He is good in the box, he is good out of the box, he is good coming to his left side, he is good with the head, he is very complete, he is intelligent. Still young, still things to develop, but many, many absolutely outstanding qualities.”

Chelsea host Hull on Saturday afternoon and will be looking for a strong home performances after fighting back from 2-0 down to beat Leeds 6-3 in the Carabao Cup on Wednesday.

Palmer was key to the comeback and revealed that Alonso, who had rotated heavily, ripped into his players at half-time against Leeds. “I was angry with myself that I didn’t help the players to play better or have a better feeling,” Alonso said. “There is a moment that you try to explain what is not working well, try to make preparations and then there is a moment that you need to kick their arse a little bit, in a nice way. It worked – not for me but the players who came on with a better quality and better everything in the second half.”

Chelsea will again be without Moisés Caicedo. The midfielder is yet to start this season and Alonso does not want to risk him. Jacob Steinberg

4. De Zerbi wants exile Richarlison to stay

Roberto De Zerbi insists he does not regret the handling of Richarlison’s situation at Tottenham after the forward was omitted from his Premier League squad, even though Spurs are yet to score in the competition.

De Zerbi said Richarlison had in effect exiled himself by refusing to sign a new contract and repeatedly saying he wanted to leave. The 29-year-old’s absence looks increasingly unfortunate for Spurs after three league matches. They have never gone four league games without scoring at the start of a season.

De Zerbi described Richarlison’s omission as a “consequence” of the Brazilian’s actions over the past month and a half. A deadline-day move to Everton, who visit the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium on Saturday, collapsed after Spurs had signed replacements. Richarlison continues to train with the first team. “If I had decided myself to leave him outside of the squad, I would have regrets,” De Zerbi said. “But the decision has not even been taken by the club.”

The Italian said it would be “much better” if Richarlison were in his squad, happy to stay and “maybe to extend his contract, because he is still an important player, he was important last season, we can’t forget. But we can’t forget also the last 45 days.”

De Zerbi is missing last season’s three top scorers: Richarlison, João Palhinha, who left for Benfica, and Cristian Romero, who joined Atlético Madrid. Mykhailo Mudryk signed on loan from Chelsea, picked up an injury in training. An ankle scan revealed ligament damage that will keep the winger out for about six weeks. De Zerbi feels the “silly injury”, caused by playing too much after being out for so long, could have been avoided.

Sávio arrived from Manchester City for £75m, closely followed by Omar Marmoush on loan. Marmoush scored only 10 league goals in a season and a half at Manchester City, but was more prolific in the Bundesliga at Eintracht Frankfurt. “In terms of goals he’s not Harry Kane but he can score more goals than he has done in the last two seasons,” De Zerbi said.

“If you analyse his qualities, he can score more goals and he has to demand more goals from himself. Even the stupid goals, he has to change his habits after being used to scoring the great goals.”

De Zerbi says his players have lacked confidence and freedom on the pitch this season and challenged them to take more risks and show personality “like a big team” and “like big players”.

Meanwhile, Lucas Bergvall has signed a new long-term contract. The 20-year-old wanted to leave in the summer but was convinced to stay by De Zerbi. Sam Cunningham

5. Manchester United take action against ticket touts

Manchester United believe they have disrupted organised ticketing networks having removed 685 season tickets as part of a contentious ticket touting investigation. The club’s summer crackdown resulted in widespread condemnations from fans and supporter groups after many innocent people faced the threat of sanction.

The 1958 this week called for fans to “stand united” against the “season ticket ban fiasco” in a protest before Sunday’s derby against Manchester City as a “line has been crossed”.

United released an outcome update on their investigation before this weekend’s action, revealing that 685 accounts have been subject to a ban while 464 supporters received a reduced sanction or final warning.

A club statement read: “Bans were issued where there was significant misuse of the ticketing system for financial gain. This included the operation of organised ticketing networks, which were controlling, selling and distributing tickets from hundreds of accounts.

“These actions undermine fair access to tickets for genuine supporters and have no place at Manchester United. Our focus now turns to ensuring these tickets are returned to our supporters. All season tickets released through this process will be offered to supporters on the season ticket waiting list.”

United say the investigation identified 1,617 accounts that required further review due to what it calls “unusual activity”. Of those stripped of season tickets, 113 failed to respond to requests for further information, 73 did not appeal and 499 received bans upheld by an independent appeals panel. Press Association

6. Jaissle hopes Fernandez-Pardo can face Leeds

Matthias Jaissle revealed that summer signing Matias Fernandez-Pardo is edging closer to starting for Newcastle. The 21-year-old forward arrived on Tyneside from Lille on deadline day and has featured as a substitute in Newcastle’s last two matches.

Speaking before Monday’s fixture with Leeds, Jaissle said: “Yeah, he’s getting closer. I said that we need to be smart with his load management. Now he’s getting more and more minutes. He has now almost a full training week to Leeds, that helps him a lot. I think it’s the first time now since he arrived, and then we can make the decision on Sunday, maybe even on Monday.”

Jaissle was also pleased to see Tino Livramento continue his return from injury as the full-back got 45 minutes of football under his belt with an appearance from the bench during the second half of Tuesday’s Carabao Cup win over Millwall.

“I’m happy for him that he got 45 minutes on a high level against a strong opponent in difficult circumstances playing there in Millwall,” the Newcastle manager said. “That makes us proud to see him already on a high level.” Press Association

7. Rose needs a win before things get Real

Marco Rose says Bournemouth must stick together to end his winless start in the Premier League before the club’s maiden European campaign begins. The south coast club have taken only two points from a possible nine under their new head coach after surrendering late leads to lose 2-1 at Manchester City and draw 1-1 with Everton and 2-2 against Newcastle.

Bournemouth, who thumped Championship club Lincoln City 4-0 in the Carabao Cup in midweek, host Brentford on Saturday before a landmark Europa League fixture away to Spanish side Real Sociedad on Thursday.

“It’s important and I would love to have it done already but it’s not the case,” Rose said of securing a first top-flight victory. “We need to work for it. We have to stick together, we have to believe in it. I think a home game with our fans is a big chance to do it and always the next game is a chance to change things, to change situations. We are quite confident.”

Bournemouth have never beaten Brentford in the Premier League, losing five and drawing three of the previous eight meetings between the clubs. “We just have to continue, so it means finding the right balance in everything,” said Rose. “We didn’t get nervous after the first results, we played quite confident, and that’s what we have to now do in the next game: believe in our qualities and our abilities.” Press Association

items.title: Anthropic blocks possible attempt to use AI to make biological weapons
items.summary: Anthropic says it has identified and disrupted attempts to use its AI model for "malicious activity" which could support the development of biological
items.text:
Anthropic says it has identified and disrupted attempts to use its AI model for "malicious activity" which could support the development of biological weapons.

The findings, made in the firm's recent threat intelligence report, is the latest in a growing series of warnings from AI researchers and industry insiders about the technology's potential risks to humanity.

The warnings have prompted calls to action, with US Senator Bernie Sanders demanding a pause on advanced AI development and a ban on artificial superintelligence.

President Donald Trump has so far rejected such fears, saying on Thursday he was concerned "if we don't win AI, we're going to be put in a very bad position".

The company published its latest threat intelligence report, external on Thursday.

Such reports have become a regular feature across the AI industry as firms seek to demonstrate how they identify and disrupt attempts to misuse their models.

This includes Google, which wrote on Tuesday, external that a person had attempted to use its AI tool, Gemini, to obtain a "complete, step-by-step technical guide for synthesizing weaponised biological agents".

Claude, Anthropic's AI model was also used by actors linked to a Russia-based cyber espionage campaign and by an Iranian propaganda institution, according to its report.

The cases of concern detected over the past eight months ranged from fake dating apps and hotel Wifi scams, to surveillance built to identify dissidents.

Anthropic has also accused Chinese AI firms of trying to replicate Claude's capabilities.

The lengthy report lists cases in which suspected state-sponsored groups, criminals, spyware vendors, state propaganda institutions and politically motivated individuals misused its technology.

"Malicious use" of its Claude Haiku, Sonnet, and Opus models was disrupted between December 2025 and August 2026, it said.

None of the misuse cases involved Claude Fable or the powerful Mythos-class models, with the exception of one instance of distillation - the process for training smaller AI models using larger, more expensive models.

As well as detecting the use of its models for cyber and influence operations, surveillance, scams and fraud and weapon development, Anthropic said it had blocked scientists who used its AI in ways that could support biological weapons development.

The report highlighted "five case studies of actors using our models in ways that could support biological weapons development".

Biological misuse, it said, is "one of the most serious risks of frontier AI model". Without the correct safeguards, such capabilities "could have catastrophic consequences", Anthropic said.

"The same information that can be used to develop a biological weapon could also be used to develop, for example, a vaccine or a cure for a disease," Anthropic said.

Jacob Klein, the head of threat intelligence at Anthropic, told the New York Times, external it was "an incredibly nuanced situation".

"You are not seeing someone in a comic book kind of way say, 'Hey, I want to build a biological weapon to kill everybody,'" he said.

The report also noted six cases where Claude was used "to develop software for conventional weapons, including firearms, missiles, armed drones, bombs, and other munitions, as well as the targeting and control systems that operate them".

The report indicated that cybercriminals and state-backed hackers have increasingly used its technology to assist their operations.

Hacking group ShinyHunters, as well as China-based labs, were among those named in the report.

The report also said that a hacking group whose work is consistent with the Russia-based Midnight Blizzard allegedly used AI to build a system that automatically detected when its malware was flagged by security defences and rewrote code until it evaded detection.

The California-based company said it had incorporated its findings into its processes "to better prevent, detect, and disrupt these activities in the future".

Anthropic said it had shared intelligence with authorities and industry partners where appropriate.

The report - the company's first this year - comes after a top safety researcher at Anthropic warned AI is advancing so quickly he believes there is a greater than 10% chance it "could kill all humans" within the next decade.

In an article published on 6 September, OpenAI chief scientist Jakub Pachocki called for the industry to implement "voluntary slowdowns" until safeguards are set.

"I am concerned no one is prepared for the consequences of a continued rapid rise in machine intelligence," Pachocki said, adding that OpenAI, which makes ChatGPT, will continue its work on building safeguards, though broader interventions are required.

The warning prompted an open letter to UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham calling for a new multinational treaty for the safe development of AI and a call for governments to collaborate about what a treaty based on the development of superintelligence should look like.

In the US, Democratic lawmaker Bernie Sanders has introduced legislation to ban AI superintelligence and temporarily pause advanced AI development.

"When scientists tell you there is a chance, a chance that it could have a cataclysmic impact on humanity, you've got be a moron not to say, slow it down," he said on Thursday on BBC's Newsnight.

With additional reporting from Osmond Chia.

items.title: Russia's new jet-powered drones outpacing Ukraine's air defences with daily launches
items.summary: Russia fired its new rapid, jet-powered drones against Ukraine every day throughout August, BBC Verify analysis of Ukrainian Air Force data has found,
items.text:
Russia fired its new rapid, jet-powered drones against Ukraine every day throughout August, BBC Verify analysis of Ukrainian Air Force data has found, escalating its use of a weapon that Kyiv's air defences are struggling to deal with.

It marked the first time that daily attacks by Moscow's new upgraded Geran drones were recorded in Ukrainian Air Force data. The growing use of jet-propelled and other varieties of drones prompted President Volodymyr Zelensky to condemn what he called an unfolding "horror" over the skies of Kyiv.

Ukraine's military recently told the BBC that jet-powered drone attacks grew from 350 in June to 1,600 in July and 2,800 in August. In five of the nightly attacks in August, these drones outnumbered the older, slower models.

"The reason for turning to jet-powered drones is that they are much faster than the previous generation and it makes it much more difficult for Ukraine to intercept them," said Dr Marina Miron, an expert on military technology at King's College London.

The upgraded munitions can cruise at more than 300mph, significantly faster than older models and well beyond the top speed of Kyiv's interceptors. The drones are powered by turbojet engines, some of which, according to Ukrainian military intelligence, are sourced from China.

According to Zelensky, the drones were used as part of a wave of attacks that killed at least 12 people and injured 20 more on 1 September. Six of the casualties were railway workers after a depot was hit in Kyiv.

And on Wednesday the Moldovan government said a plane carrying Zelensky was delayed at Chisinau airport on Tuesday after a Russian drone - reported to be jet-powered - entered Moldovan airspace.

Earlier this year Ukraine showed relative success in countering Russian drones and was intercepting 94% of long-range drones, according to Zelensky. But the speed of the newer drones has prompted the latest round in Kyiv and Moscow's arms race. On 10 August, Ukraine's deputy head of military intelligence, Maj Gen Vadym Skibitskyi, said his forces needed new interceptor missiles "capable of matching [jet-drones'] speed".

Four Ukrainian companies have reportedly started testing missiles that can shoot down the new Geran models, officials in Kyiv recently told reporters. The country's new defence minister, Yevhenii Khmara, has tasked them with producing "thousands of units" as quickly as possible.

Russia also had an economic incentive to invest in the jet-powered drones. The increased speed and manoeuvrability of these models means the line between them and more expensive cruise missiles has become "blurred", said John Hardie of the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, a think tank focused on national security and foreign policy.

"Long-range one-way attack drones are basically a poor man's cruise missile," he said. "The more you add capability to a drone, the less meaningful the distinction between the drone and a lower-end cruise missile."

But the analyst organisation Conflict Armament Research emphasised that jet-drones are not yet as advanced as cruise missiles. It said the munitions have a shorter attack range, carry much smaller warheads and are more susceptible to jamming systems.

Meanwhile, satellite images appear to show Moscow is redesigning key facilities dedicated to fighting the war in Ukraine to host jet-powered drones, with longer rails associated with the munitions visible at an entirely new base at Tsymbulova in the Oryol region.

Multiple launch sites appear to have been built at the facility, which is around 109 miles (175 km) from the Ukrainian border.

Since the facility became operational, Tsymbulova appears to have become a key centre for Russian drone attacks. Oryol region, where the Tsymbulova base is located, was not mentioned as a drone launch site in Air Force reports before September 2024, but by August 2026 it was named in almost every attack.

The proliferation of jet-powered drones comes as BBC Verify found that Russia is now striking Ukraine with complex attacks involving hundreds of drones and missiles about once a week.

The increase in the size of the strikes is being powered by Moscow's shift towards combining a "greater variety of munitions" - including jet-powered and decoy drones - with expensive ballistic missiles that are extremely difficult to intercept, analyst Michael Bohnert of the RAND think tank told BBC Verify. Kyiv's data shows that Moscow is now using over 15 times as many drones per attack than it was four years ago.

Bohnert added that the tactically complicated nature of the assaults, coupled with a global shortage of air defence systems capable of halting ballistic missiles partly caused by the US-Israeli war with Iran, has led to falling interception rates by Ukraine.

Ukraine's Air Force data showed a drop in interceptions of ballistic missiles up to the end of July. In August, Kyiv mostly stopped publishing the figures that would show its interception rate.

We believe that this incident was the result of an OpenAI agent swarm. Our main sources of evidence are:

The packages are clearly LLM-authored. We ran some of the malicious packages through Pangram, which detected them as 100% AI generated. This is evidence that the attack was an agent swarm (but not that it originates from OpenAI).

Agents self-identified as being from OpenAI. Hundreds of the packages that were uploaded contain “oai” in their name. Fifteen of the packages set “oai” as their author. Another lists an email for contact as “openaixyz65947@gmail.com”.

The swarm behaves extremely similarly to the German-wiki agents we previously found.

The June agents were accessing 49 of the same files as the wiki agents, which OpenAI has confirmed were theirs.

The May agents were accessing different files (mostly local UK government data), but these files are very similar in character to those pursued by the wiki agents. Moreover, they use the same retrieval methods. 1,397 packages mention r.jina.ai, which was used heavily by the agents on the wiki. We also see that many packages mention example.com, which wiki agents used to test their posting ability.

Our understanding from talking to people in the RubyGems community is that OpenAI never informed them that they were responsible for this attack.

Note: After publishing this report, we were informed that X user @she_llac independently discovered that the agents were using RubyGems’ build system in order to fetch packages and shared this on Discord prior to us publishing. We’re grateful for @she_llac’s work in both discovering this and in coordinating a community of people to look for more rogue agents.

Whenever you publish a package (also known as a gem) to RubyGems, and submit a request, the site RubyDoc.info builds and hosts documentation for it.

The process of building documentation for a gem involves evaluating a user-specified `.yardopts` file, which allows linking to Ruby scripts intended to help with this process. In the GemStuffer campaign, the agents abused this to gain arbitrary remote code execution on the RubyDoc.info’s servers.

We know that this was the intended pathway of the agents because they (rather transparently) told us so.

In the now-rescinded gem zzsouthrunner (which notably shares the ZZ naming scheme that both the wiki agents and Huggingface ones used), the agents leave the following comment on top of the linked payload:

# malicious crawler/exfil for Southwark Jan 2026 docs via rubydoc.info worker

We know that over a hundred packages used the following exploitation path:

Submit a malicious package to RubyGems

Trigger a documentation request, so that RubyDoc.info will build the package

Use the build script to run code on RubyDoc.info and scrape target websites

Exfiltrate the data off RubyDoc.info’s servers by publishing another gem back to the RubyGems package registry, which is publicly viewable.

Additionally, once the AIs got arbitrary RCE on the build environment, they would sometimes use the build environment to attempt to steal other users’ API keys (though we are unsure if they succeeded or not). This is discussed more in the following section.

The agents clearly regarded what they were doing as hacking. Agents used file names like hack.rb, evil.rb, inject.rb, exploit.rb, and ssrf.rb. (SSRF stands for “Server-Side Request Forgery”, a type of security vulnerability). They also dubbed packages conspicuous titles like pwnp999, exfiltestwand3, hacksvn1778554764, and lambproxyhackabcxyz. Comments such as “# malicious probe” or “#hack” are littered across the campaign.

At some points, the agents attempted to be covert. We found multiple packages that would disarm themselves to hide their payload in the next version. They uploaded one package with the comment “# disable evil in next version and bump version”, which after execution would modify the package to remove the malicious code initially inserted. Another such package (lambethcalcqzewgt) follows the same self-disarming pattern. (Fortunately, they still uploaded these files and comments publicly, so they were not very successful at their “covert” behavior).

items.title: A Design Space Exploration of Async/Await
items.author: wcrichton
items.summary: Many programming languages now provide the async/await keywords for expressing concurrency. The design rationale is pretty consistent: to make concurrent
items.text:
Many programming languages now provide the async/await keywords for expressing concurrency. The design rationale is pretty consistent: to make concurrent programs look more like straight-line code (see: Python, Rust, or Swift). We therefore describe the paradigm which encompasses async/await as straight-line asynchrony, as opposed to using event loops or callbacks.

Language designs for straight-line asynchrony have been brewing for over 15 years. In this project, we wanted to understand: how similar or different is async/await between languages? The short answer is a lot more different than we expected. We wrote a paper, “A Design Space Exploration of Async/Await”, to explain how.

So you think you know async/await?

To demonstrate how much modern languages can diverge, here’s a small async program written in pseudocode. One function writes to a log, and another fires off the log write as a background task and moves on.

async fn write_to_log():
print("A")
// simulate a slow log write
await sleep(2)
print("B")
async fn fire_and_forget():
task = spawn write_to_log()
// return without awaiting the task
async fn main():
await fire_and_forget()
await sleep(1)
print("C")

What would you expect this program to print?

There isn’t really a right answer, because you were probably right for some language. Below is how seven modern async runtimes actually behave:

Four different answers, for a program whose entire job is to write a log line in the background. And it gets worse. In the paper, we show that across the seven runtimes, no two produce the same output for three variations of this simple program!

Do you actually know your language’s async semantics?

Why the disagreement?

While watching videos from a programming influencer you may have have heard the terms “cold” or “hot” async function calls. The idea is that “hot starts” return a task that is immediately running in the runtime, while “cold starts” return an inert object that does nothing until awaited.

Hot vs. cold functions is what we call an async design dimension: a design decision that affects the observable semantics of program execution (as opposed to matters of pure performance). We call this particular dimension “Eagerness”, and in the paper we identify nine such dimensions from modern implementations of straight-line asynchrony. Below we’ve grouped these nine dimension into three categories that roughly correspond to the lifetime of a task: Start of Life, End of Life, and Cancellation.

Click a language to trace its design choices through the table.

Start of Life

How to evaluate an async function application.

Americans don’t agree on much, but that’s not the case when it comes to data centers.

​Seven in 10 Americans oppose building data centers for artificial intelligence in or near their communities. Despite this, the federal government is moving to make it easier for them to be built. And in some places, residents won’t even get the chance to raise concerns publicly or even know if a data center is coming to their neighborhoods.

The federal Environmental Protection Agency plans to scrap a federal requirement that states tell the public — and allow public comment — before approving air-pollution permits for industrial facilities. That includes the data centers rising across the country, as well as the power plants built to feed their enormous appetite for electricity.

At the same time, the EPA last month also proposed another change that would let developers start building data centers before their permits are approved.

The rural South, which is home to a disproportionate amount of Black communities, has seen the largest growth of these large data centers. The proposals and lack of transparency may worsen health risks, increase utility bills, and contribute to community displacement, residents told Capital B.

​The change at the federal level would mean that, in some places, residents could lose one of their few formal chances to ask questions, raise alarms, or learn that a data center is headed their way before the permits are signed and construction begins.

Paul Black, an environmental activist organizing against a data center complex the size of 1,200 football fields in rural South Carolina, said these moves “run counter to the way American democracy is sold to us.”

“It is a betrayal of everything that this country should stand for, purports to stand for. It runs counter to the will of the people,” he added.

The data center project currently being debated in his 40% Black community was only proposed there after developers tried — and failed — to build a similar campus in a predominantly white county in Georgia.​

​The change at the federal level would mean that, in some places, residents could lose one of their few formal chances to ask questions, raise alarms, or learn that a data center is headed their way before the permits are signed and construction begins.

In a statement, the EPA said the proposal would “provide the state and local agencies most familiar with local issues the discretion to determine whether, when, and for how long to provide opportunities for public participation.”

But many Americans are increasingly losing faith in their local governments to work in their best interests.

In part of a growing web of secrecy, local governments have routinely signed nondisclosure agreements with tech companies to hide these projects and overruled legal orders in order to bury information about them.

“What I am saying is that if we, as the community, the people who are responsible, can’t understand this, can’t have questions answered, can’t have information, then how can I look somebody in the eye and tell them this is good for you, trust me?” Davante Lewis, a Louisiana public service commissioner tasked with regulating industry, told Capital B last month.

Lewis was the only member to vote in favor of releasing electricity use information tied to the current construction of the country’s largest data center in rural Louisiana.

Nearly 200 advocacy groups and more than a dozen states, led by both Democrats and Republicans, have voiced opposition to the federal changes.

Where the biggest threats lie

​“In the more rural parts of the nation, we are under attack by data centers,” Black said. “They are seeking to get in as fast as possible, as quietly as possible, and do what they will to the places [where] we live, that we find precious, the places that we’ve preserved, and they want to come in in the dark of the night to build a data center.”

Last month, South Carolina passed its own ruling that says power plants for data centers can be constructed without review or approval from the state’s regulatory commission.

The burden of data center growth is already falling heavily on Black communities. Data centers can drive demand for gas-fired power plants and turbines, which emit smog-forming nitrogen oxides, fine particulate matter and, in some cases, hazardous air pollutants such as formaldehyde connected to a slew of cancers.

“It’s beyond cruel for Trump’s EPA to silence front-line communities who bear the brunt of unhealthy air,” said Brandon Jones-Cobb, a senior attorney at the Center for Biological Diversity.

At the same time, the costs of building new utility infrastructure is often passed onto ratepayers. Black households, who on average face a higher energy burden than other groups, have been plagued by rising bills and subsequently power shutoffs related to data center growth.

Industrial growth can also remake housing markets faster than rural communities can absorb. In communities surrounding where Meta is constructing the nation’s largest data center, a local mayor told Capital B that prices had doubled and families in trailer-home parks had been evicted to make room for higher-earning construction workers. The area’s median home and rental prices rose 80% in just one year.

The EPA said the proposed changes would “responsibly speed up permitting, supporting American economic development and energy dominance.”

Last year, Lee Zeldin, who runs the EPA, said it was now the agency’s top priority to “make the United States the artificial intelligence capital of the world.” The 56-year-old agency was established in 1970 to protect the environment and public health.

“The level of unequalness with these data centers cannot be understated,” Black said. “The government is rewriting the rules and the richest corporations in the world are supporting them so that one of our only ways to make our voices heard is erased.”

The EPA is expected to finalize the proposal within the next year.

items.text:
Over the last few months, the mathematical capabilities of LLMs have improved dramatically, to the point that they can solve major outstanding problems in many fields of mathematics. However, the push by AI companies to solve mathematical problems as a benchmark is detrimental to the science of mathematics, and to the mathematical community. The goals of the AI companies and the goals of the mathematical community are severely misaligned. We see these as part of broader alignment issues impacting other scientific and creative professions, as well as the whole of society.

Research mathematics deals with understanding basic structures of shapes, numbers, and natural phenomena. Over the course of generations, it has built a large corpus of sophisticated ideas, methods, abstractions, and other tools to comprehend the mathematical landscape. In turn, modern technologies and sciences are based on mathematical tools.

Famous problems have often served as landmarks and lighthouses against which one can measure an improved understanding of this landscape. Solving one of these problems has been a certain sign of new insights and interesting methods, which would then be studied by a community of mathematicians, through a long and arduous process of talks, discussions, simplifications. At the end of this process, one will ideally find a textbook presentation of the results suitable for any graduate or even undergraduate student to study. Some of the mathematical ideas pursue their journey even further to become, decades or centuries after, tools that are understood and used by the whole population.

The mathematical community functions, in many ways, as a miniature version of humanity. It consists of individuals using a wide variety of different approaches, joined by core values. The most precious resources of our profession are students and ideas, and these we nurture with great care. We feel responsible to let them grow to their full potential, until they can live a life of their own in the mathematical world. For students we often suggest problems with the core intention of developing skills making them well-positioned for advances in research and elsewhere. Our ideas we disseminate in talks, private discussions and careful writeups, connecting them to the previous ideas of others. These processes invariably take time and are based on human interaction.

In recent months, the success of AI in solving major mathematical problems has made headlines even outside mathematical circles. But solving problems is only a tool and proxy for achieving the primary goal of conceptual understanding and insight. Forgetting this in the world of AI may turn the tool against the primary goal. Indeed, the mass production at faster and faster pace of "true/false" statements could destroy fertile ground instead of breathing life into new ideas.

Often these solutions are announced in a rush, leaving no time for a proper writeup, the isolation of new methods and ideas, and citing relevant previous work of others. As in all creative professions, this raises severe attribution and plagiarism questions. Moreover, without the willing mathematicians who must take care of their development and integration into the mathematical canon, AI-conceived ideas would never become fully alive and the crucial human transmission chain between mathematicians would be lost.

We are witnessing a general threat to intellectual work, with misalignment between the outcome of the use of AI and its initial purpose. In many fields and activities, years of training have traditionally served not only to produce a final answer or product, but also to develop understanding and the ability to formulate new questions and ideas. However, building on a vast body of previous human work, AI systems are becoming increasingly capable of producing the results of such work directly, and these goals cease to align. The issues the mathematical community faces now are similar to issues that other scientific and creative professions are facing, and indicate issues that all of humanity might face: how to make sure that, as AI changes the way work is done, we do not lose sight of what that work was meant to achieve in the first place.

AI offers the potential of enhancing and accelerating genuine mathematical study and understanding. Mathematics as a profession will need to adapt to these changes in several ways. However, whether these changes ultimately benefit the field or have a destructive effect will in large part be determined by the decisions of the humans in control of this new technology.

These issues must be addressed urgently, in the mathematical community, by the companies developing these technologies and, more broadly, by a society that will confront similar problems in many other forms of intellectual work.
